#6130. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6129. United Airlines’ Oldest Aircraft Is Over 30 Years Old & It’s Still Going Strong In 2026

United Airlines is keeping a large contingent of three-decade-old widebodies flying across long-haul skies in 2026, led by active flagship N641UA at 35.72 years old. Data from ch-aviation lists 37 Boeing 767-300ER aircraft in United's fleet, with 20 airframes aged 30 years and older, 18 active, one in maintenance, and one in storage. It would be so easy to go and sideline these seasoned twin-aisle jets, but United continues to rely on them for demanding international and domestic flying.

How can three-decade-old widebodies remain central to a major global carrier's network in 2026 when newer twinjets are already in service and improve on every metric? Looking at ch-aviation fleet records alongside recent flight activity and industry coverage, this article examines United's 30-plus Boeing 767-300ER airframes, cabin configurations, retirement plans, rival widebody comparisons, and the operational economics keeping them airborne.

According to ch-aviation fleet records from November 19, 2026, 20 of United Airlines's 767-300ER airframes are aged 30 years and older, spanning from 33.27 years up to 35.72 years. At the top of that age bracket sits active flagship N641UA at 35.72 years, followed closely by active N642UA at 35.61 years and active twins N644UA and N643UA at 35.58 years apiece. Seventeen other airframes in this cohort sit between 33.27 and 34.69 years, with 18 of the 20 aircraft active, N648UA in maintenance at 34.41 years, and N659UA in storage at 33.7 years.

Closely following specific tail numbers from this 30-plus group shows how actively these airframes still work long-haul and domestic rotations in late 2026. FlightAware records show N641UA operating long-distance flights such as Houston (IAH) to Santiago (SCL), a 4,669-mile (7,514-km) sector, and Amsterdam (AMS), while FlightAware shows N642UA rotating between Washington Dulles (IAD), Houston, Amsterdam, and South America. Even N644UA returned to active line flying in November 2026 after diverting to St. John's (YYT) over an engine issue on a Washington Dulles–Amsterdam flight in October 2026.

Having 18 30-plus 767-300ERs actively flying alongside two others in maintenance or storage highlights how central older aircraft are to daily dispatch reliability. Routine maintenance checks on jets like N648UA and occasional short-term storage on N659UA form a normal part of running a mature fleet rather than suggesting an immediate fleetwide grounding.

United Airlines has outfitted its fleet of 767-300ERs with modern long-haul cabins tailored to high-yield demand. According to United Airlines's fleet specifications, the carrier operates two distinct three-cabin layouts on the type, combining lie-flat Polaris business seats with United Premium Plus, Economy Plus, and standard economy. Even on older fuselages, passengers get onboard WiFi, in-seat power outlets, USB ports, and seatback audio-video on demand across every cabin.

The flagship high-J configuration packs 167 seats into the fuselage, led by 46 Polaris suites with 77 inches (195 cm) of sleeping space, 22 Premium Plus recliners offering 38 inches (96 cm) of pitch and six inches (15 cm) of recline, 43 Economy Plus seats and 56 economy seats arranged in a passenger-friendly 2-3-2 layout. A second 203-seat version caters more to corporate and leisure demand with 30 Polaris seats, 24 Premium Plus seats, and 149 Economy seats, where Economy Plus offers 34 inches (86 cm) of pitch and standard economy provides 31 inches (79 cm) of pitch with 18.5-inch (46.9-cm) seat widths.

That cabin mix makes the 767-300ER uniquely suited to transatlantic and secondary international routes where larger twinjets would carry too many empty seats. Deploying the 167-seat premium-heavy variant on business-dense European routes out of hubs like Newark and Chicago while assigning the 203-seat version to mixed leisure-and-corporate corridors, United extracts strong revenue per departure. Combined with its comfortable 2-3-2 cross-section, the modernized interior explains why passengers and schedulers alike still value the type.

Have you ever wondered why the carrier is still flying aircraft up to 30 years old?

United Airlines plans to be well into retiring its 767 fleet around 2030, setting a clear multi-year horizon for winding down the type. The aircraft will not be grounded abruptly, as management has framed the exit around fleet renewal and long-haul capacity growth as newer twinjets enter service. That timeline gives United room to extract remaining value from its 767s while preparing replacement capacity.

Boeing 787 Dreamliners sit at the center of that transition as United's primary long-term widebody replacement, an aircraft that has been integral to the airline's growth in recent years. With 787-9 and expanded 787-10 deliveries rolling out across upcoming fleet waves, resulting in the airline becoming the largest 787 operator globally, United gains far better fuel efficiency, lower operating costs, and upgraded premium cabins than older twin-aisle jets can match. Shifting transatlantic and trunk widebody flying onto Dreamliners lets United retire aging airframes a step at a time, not infringing on long-haul frequency.

Deliveries and widebody fleet planning still carry moving parts as United looks toward the end of the decade. Supply-chain pacing, aircraft delivery schedules, and long-range fleet choices, including whether United ever firms up its long-delayed Airbus A350 order around 2030, will shape how quickly 767s exit, though that seems highly unlikely as of November 2026. Until enough replacements arrive in full volume, the 767 is integral to the United fleet.

United Airlines is far from alone in flying mature 767-300ERs, with Delta Air Lines running a similarly seasoned widebody subfleet. Across 37 Boeing 767-300ERs, Delta's average fleet age stood at 29.7 years in September 2026, closely tracking United's 29.8-year average across 37 aircraft of the same variant at the end of 2025, as per data from AeroCorner.

Other airlines show contrasting ways of handling aging 767s as market demand and new deliveries shift. Air Canada retired its passenger 767s in 2020 before moving to reintroduce two stored 767-300ERs as short-term capacity insurance while adjusting 767 freighter plans around incoming Dreamliners and Airbus widebodies. Meanwhile, lease-heavy low-cost carriers such as Frontier rely on operating leases to keep average fleet ages young rather than holding decades-old jets.

Comparing United against Delta, Air Canada, and lease-focused rivals helps to show more clearly how ownership structure and hub economics drive widebody longevity. Where ultra-low-cost operators avoid ownership exposure and rapid-growth airlines lean on newer deliveries, legacy carriers with established transatlantic and long-haul hubs can squeeze extra years out of 767-300ERs. That contrast highlights why United's approach looks distinctly legacy-carrier-like.

Discover the oldest jets in the largest US airline fleets.

Keeping 30-year-old 767-300ERs flying is not as straightforward as it is with newer aircraft. Older airframes demand thorough heavy checks, corrosion inspections, and component overhauls as flight hours and cycles climb, but paid-off ownership and lower capital charges can still make them profitable on seasonal or peak-demand routes. When peak revenue outpaces incremental fuel and maintenance spend, keeping an older widebody on the line makes a lot of financial sense.

At the same time, the broader 767 program is entering its final commercial chapter as Boeing winds down commercial 767 production in 2027 after completing remaining freighter orders. Even as commercial assembly ends in Everett, while KC-46A tanker production continues, hundreds of existing 767s will remain active in passenger, freighter, and converted cargo service for many years. Spare-parts support and mature maintenance ecosystems are naturally vital for operators running the type deep into its fourth decade.

For long-haul twinjet flying more broadly, the 767-300ER's staying power shows how mid-sized widebodies fill a practical niche between narrowbodies and larger twinjets. Where replacement widebodies face tight delivery slots or higher upfront acquisition costs, well-maintained 767-300ERs buy airlines schedule flexibility and capacity cushion. That combination of proven range, familiar operations, and practical economics explains why 30-plus-year-old airframes are still going strong in 2026.

United Airlines's 30-plus 767-300ER fleet shows that age alone does not sideline a well-supported widebody when economics and network fit align. Across 37 airframes in ch-aviation records, 20 aircraft aged 30 years and older, led by active flagship N641UA at 35.72 years, continue flying demanding routes thanks to updated Polaris and Premium Plus cabins, paid-off ownership, and practical mid-sized widebody economics. Many airlines would see these aircraft as simple stopgaps, but these veteran twinjets carry real commercial weight on routes where larger twinjets would carry excess capacity.

The 767 story at United is unfortunately not forever lasting. Boeing is winding down commercial 767 production, and around 2030, United targets retiring its 767 fleet as 787 Dreamliners take over. Only time will tell how smoothly those Dreamliner deliveries ramp up, how spare parts and maintenance support hold up after commercial assembly ends, and how reliably 30-plus airframes perform across upcoming seasons.

Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

First, map out your holiday shopping plans and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you plan to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

For example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

Statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

We talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

By doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

We suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

No matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers

We’re big fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

Paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on new purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a plan to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

Another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Plan It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

Holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can quickly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

#6126. Not Again: Cargo Jet Overruns Miami Airport Runway (This Time A FedEx MD-11)

Miami International Airport (MIA) is having a bad luck streak when it comes to cargo planes being able to stay on the runway, but at least this time around there were no fatalities. Still, yikes…

At 8:25PM on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport, leading the airport to be shut down for an extended period of time.

The 34-year-old MD-11 with the registration code N605FE had just performed flight FX910 from Memphis (MEM), and was coming in to land on runway 26R, which is 9,355 feet (2,851 meters) long. That’s a solidly long runway, for what it’s worth.

However, the plane wasn’t able to stop before the end of the runway, and seemed to exit the paved surface at a speed of around 50 knots, and came to a stop around 320 meters (1,000 feet) past the end of the runway, right by the airport perimeter fence.

🚨 USA | FEDEX CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS RUNWAY AT #MIAMI AIRPORT!MD-11 arriving from Memphis skidded into the grass beyond Runway 26R, triggering an FAA ground stop.2 crew members are safe. No deaths or injuries.#FlaPanthers #Survivor51 #ไฟไหม้ pic.twitter.com/kTM48GkeGf

WATCH: FedEx cargo plane in the grass after overshooting runway at Miami International Airport pic.twitter.com/t4DPQwUb0m

Fortunately there were no serious injuries. There’s video footage showing stairs being pulled up to the plane, and the pilots walking off with their bags. There’s always the classic aviation adage that “any landing you can walk away from is a good one,” and if that’s the case, I guess this was a good landing.

Footage showing the FedEx Express MD-11F after it overran the runway at Miami International Airport tonight. As a result of the incident, a ground stop was issued. pic.twitter.com/ldraejGQ4v

This accident ended up causing a ground stop of nearly two hours at the airport. That’s not exactly ideal timing, given what a busy travel day yesterday was, ahead of Thanksgiving. Operations did eventually resume, but with delays averaging over three hours.

🚨 迈阿密国际机场关闭！今晚，一架联邦快递（FedEx）货运飞机在迈阿密国际机场（MIA）冲出跑道，机场目前已实施地面停飞令（Ground Stop）。根据空中交通管制（ATC）的录音，飞机冲出跑道后，管制员通知其他飞行员，机场“刚刚关闭”。这是今年迈阿密国际机场发生的第二起货运飞机冲出跑道事故。…

Of course the concept of a plane overrunning a runway at Miami Airport is fresh on people’s minds, given the September 6 accident we saw with a 21 Air (Amazon Air) Boeing 767-300 that overran runway 30. Tragically that accident claimed five lives, as the plane ran through the perimeter fence, and killed motorists. What we’ve found out about the piloting of that flight since the accident, and just how recklessly the captain was flying the plane, is astounding.

We’ll have to wait for a full investigation to know what happened (the NTSB typically releases a preliminary report within a month), but in terms of circumstances and possible contributing factors, there are a couple of things we know.

First, there’s footage showing the plane’s approach, and it makes it pretty clear that the plane touched down extremely late.

JUST IN: FedEx cargo plane overruns the runway at Miami International Airport. Flights halted pic.twitter.com/PFFH0TNpe1

A recreation of the approach based on flight tracking data shows just how late the plane touched down, and the big question is why the pilots didn’t perform a go around.

🚨 BREAKING: FedEx FDX910, an MD-11F registered N605FE, went off the end of runway 26R landing at Miami International from Memphis at about 8:28 PM local, Nov 25. Tower sent the next arrival around and ground control closed the airport. No injuries reported so far. pic.twitter.com/IhRUGEVR97

It’s also worth pointing out that weather in the region was really bad at the time of the accident. Anna Giaritelli, a reputable aviation journalist with good sources, quotes a Miami air traffic controller, who told her that “this was absolutely the most dangerous operation I’ve seen,” as much of the traffic approaching Miami had run into a “black hole of weather.”

A Miami air traffic controller sent me this chilling text minutes before the FedEx incident in MIA tonight(Controller was not on duty while texting me.) pic.twitter.com/Fvy7vb7xuP

It doesn’t seem like conditions at Miami Airport as such were that awful (compared to reports of severe turbulence in the region), but I imagine the bad weather could’ve contributed to a sense of “get-there-itis” for the pilots.

While this is of course unfortunate, the great news here is the lack of injuries or fatalities. The plane ended up coming to a stop just feet from the airport’s perimeter fence, and if it had crashed through that, the outcome could’ve been completely different, with fatalities among motorists.

It also has to be acknowledged that the pilots seemingly turned the plane a little bit left off the end of the runway, to avoid the localizer antenna. So at least the overrun was handled as well as it could be.

Based on the preliminary information we have so far, DEI does not appear to be a factor in this accident. 😉

A FedEx MD-11 overran the runway at Miami Airport last night, and ended up in the grass just short of the airport perimeter fence. Fortunately there were no major injuries, and the pilots managed to walk off the plane. This had major operational impacts for the airport, as a ground stop was issued, delaying lots of travelers.

Unlike the 21 Air Boeing 767 accident we saw in September, there were no fatalities this time around. Either way, two cargo planes going off Miami runways in under three months is not great.

#6125. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

#6124. How Munich Airport Clears A Runway Of Snow In Just 30 Minutes With 175 Vehicles

With 170 vehicles and 540 personnel available for winter operations, Munich Airport (MUC) is equipped to clear each runway of snow within 30 minutes. These crews remain on standby around the clock from early November to mid-April, covering the months with the highest risk of heavy snow.

MUC has reached this level of readiness in collaboration with local agricultural and trucking companies. Up to 180 people can be deployed during the night shift, with the aim of keeping the runway clear of snow, ready for operations to begin in the morning.

MUC is so eager to show off its winter operations because of how difficult it is to keep a major international airport clear and running during the winter months. The airport includes two runways, with additional aprons and taxiways. This amounts to approximately 60.3 million square feet (5.6 million square meters), or 780 football fields.

Despite the astonishing amount of real estate MUC must keep clear to avoid delays and cancellations, the airport believes it is up to the task because it can clear each runway in just 30 minutes. It does this by deploying a fleet of 21 snow blowers, five loading snow blowers, and one snow groomer. Farmers in the local area can also be called in with snowplow-equipped tractors.

MUC adds brains to the grunt task of clearing so much tarmac. Air traffic control manages the deployment and coordination of snow-clearing teams. They make use of the latest weather information and an early-warning system that intelligently predicts when icy conditions could cause a problem.

Clear runways are pointless if the jets at an airport are too iced up to take off safely. MUC also has this accounted for with winter maintenance teams who use 'Polar Bear' de-icing vehicles, which are operated in partnership with Lufthansa. The equipment deploys de-icing fluid to ensure that a jet's wings and fuselage aren't covered in ice and snow, which could prove disastrous.

To get into the right position to deploy the fluid, the tallest 'Polar Bear' is 50 feet and 10 inches (15.5 m) tall. The maintenance team at MUC has to carefully drive these huge vehicles into the optimum position. Nadine Adden, the only woman working with the polar bears, spoke to Munich Airport's news team. She said that:

"Only when the engines and the aircraft are completely free of ice and moisture can they take off safely. (...) It's like using an oversized hairdryer. (...) I have a really cool job."

MUC hasn't always been a leading airport when it comes to dealing with extreme winter conditions. The airport closed twice in quick succession during the winter of 2023 after multiple days of heavy snow. On December 5, there were no takeoffs or landings from 6:00 AM to 12:00 PM. The remainder of the day saw many more flights canceled or severely delayed. Lufthansa asked its passengers to stay at home in response.

The weekend before, freezing conditions had struck Europe and affected more flight operations at Munich Airport. Flight operations did not resume until 6:00 AM on Sunday, with some restrictions remaining in place for long after. Other airports impacted by this cold spell included Glasgow Airport (GLA) and Edinburgh Airport (EDI), while heavy snow in Oslo in April 2023 caused around 60 flight cancellations.

Closures like these show why Munich Airport has invested so heavily in protecting itself from the worst winter conditions. Anything less carries a serious risk of extensive delays and cancellations, scuppering travelers' plans over the festive season and causing enormous economic damage.

Welcome bonus: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve is an excellent card for long-term travelers because it earns at least 4 points per dollar spent on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar spent on dining purchases.

The card's up-to-$300 annual travel credit is straightforward to use, while Chase Sapphire and Priority Pass lounge access can provide a place to work, eat and recharge between flights. The card also charges no foreign transaction fees.

Its travel protections are another reason why it's a great choice for digital nomads. Baggage delay coverage, for example, can help cover essentials when your checked bag doesn't arrive on time. Trip delay and trip cancellation/interruption coverage can also soften the financial hit when plans unravel.

Plus, Chase Sapphire Reserve cardholders can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to hotel and airline partners, including fan favorites like United MileagePlus and World of Hyatt.

However, the card carries a $795 annual fee, and several of its statement credits are tied to particular merchants.

Cardholders can get up to $500 in statement credits each calendar year for qualifying prepaid stays of at least two nights through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, with a maximum of $250 per transaction. It can be a fantastic perk when a long trip calls for a comfortable hotel reset between apartment stays or after a long-haul flight.

If you spend most of the year outside the U.S., weigh the $795 annual fee against the benefits you’ll use regularly.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

The is best for digital nomads who can use its extensive lounge network, hotel elite status and premium perks.

Welcome bonus: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards Points after spending $12,000 on purchases within the first six months of card membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The Amex Platinum comes offers one of the largest airport lounge networks available. The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes access to Centurion Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required for Priority Pass Select).

That pairs nicely with a high earning rate on flights booked directly with the airline as well as up to a $200 airline fee statement credit every calendar year on your selected qualifying airline (enrollment required; terms apply).

Cardmembers can transfer their Membership Rewards points to Amex's airline and hotel partners, opening up award flights and hotel stays worldwide.

Several other card benefits lend themselves nicely to travelers who stay in hotels, rather than long-term rentals. Hotel elite status, including Hilton Honors Gold Elite, Leaders Club Sterling and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite, can make your stays more comfortable (enrollment required).

The up-to-$600 annual lodging statement credit adds more value to the card and can give you an excuse to add luxe stays to your itinerary. It is split into two up to $300 semiannual credits and applies to qualifying prepaid Airbnb Luxe, Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings through American Express Travel®. (Airbnb Luxe and THC require a minimum two-night stay; FHR will also require a minimum two-night stay beginning Jan. 1, 2027; terms apply).

It's worth noting that you likely won't be able to use every statement credit. Someone spending a lot of time outside the U.S. may have trouble using several U.S.-focused perks, including Uber Cash (for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders) and Walmart+.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum.

The Venture X is best for digital nomads who want premium travel perks and simple rewards on everyday spending.

Welcome bonus: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

For digital nomads, the Venture X works well because of how little strategy it requires, at home or abroad. It earns 2 miles per dollar spent on purchases outside bonus categories. These flat-rate, hassle-free rewards are useful when your spending habits change from one country to the next.

The card allows you to transfer your miles to 15-plus airline and hotel partners. That's even more flexibility when your travels take you all over the world.

The card's $300 annual Capital One travel credit and 10,000 anniversary miles (worth $100 toward bookings made through the Capital One Travel portal) are very easy ways to offset the annual fee.

Primary cardholders also receive complimentary access to Capital One Lounges, Capital One Landings and participating Priority Pass lounges.

The card offers cellphone protection when you pay your monthly wireless bill with it (up to $800 per eligible claim, with a $50 deductible and a maximum of two claims per 12-month period). That's useful when your phone is your boarding pass, map and connection to work.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

The offers a useful middle ground for digital nomads who want strong everyday rewards without paying a hefty annual fee.

Welcome bonus: Earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months.

At $95 a year, the Strata Premier is the easiest card on this list to justify. Its protections are particularly practical when you live out of a suitcase. The card's 24-month extended warranty can be especially useful when living on the road, as nomadic life can take a toll on electronics and other gear.

Cardholders can transfer ThankYou points to more than 20 airline and hotel partners. There's also an annual $100 hotel benefit per calendar year for a single hotel stay (of $500 or more; excluding taxes and fees) booked through CitiTravel.com or by calling Citi. That's a fast way to offset the card's $95 annual fee.

The Strata Premier offers fewer statement credits than pricier cards. Its $95 annual fee makes it a good fit if you’re traveling on a budget or want an affordable second card.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata Premier.

The is best for everyday spending abroad, thanks to its earning rate on eligible foreign transactions.

Welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first 90 days from account opening.

For digital nomads, the card's value comes from a benefit that applies well beyond Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines flights. Cardholders earn 3 Atmos Rewards points per dollar spent on foreign transactions, whether that's a hotel stay, meal, pharmacy visit or souvenir.

You'll also get a 10% rewards bonus on points earned from card purchases if you have an eligible Bank of America account.

Atmos Rewards points can be redeemed for flights on Oneworld carriers and other airline partners, in addition to Alaska and Hawaiian.

The annual Global Companion Award provides a 25,000-point discount when two travelers book award travel on the same itinerary. Based on our valuations, this benefit alone is worth $400. That's enough to justify the annual fee, even if you never touch the other Alaska or Hawaiian-specific benefits.

Cardholders who spend $60,000 in a card anniversary year can earn an additional Global Companion Award worth up to 100,000 points. Since these awards can be used in any class of service, the larger award could be particularly valuable for a premium-cabin or long-haul partner redemption.

That same $60,000 in spending earns 30,000 status points. Combined with the 10,000 status points awarded after each account anniversary, you'd have enough for Atmos Gold status (mapped to Oneworld Sapphire). On eligible itineraries, that's good for business-class lounge access — even when you're flying economy — priority check-in and boarding, preferred seating and extra baggage.

To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Summit card.

Many long-term travelers and digital nomads run businesses from the road. These travelers may find it useful to have one or more business cards as well.

One business card that's particularly well-suited to this lifestyle is the (see rates and fees).

This card earns 3 points per dollar spent on travel, shipping, social media and search engine advertising, and cable, internet and phone services (on the first $150,000 in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

The Ink Business Preferred also offers cellphone insurance, primary rental car insurance on business-related rentals and no foreign transaction fees.

To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred.

When you live out of a suitcase, the best card benefits aren't always flashy. What matters is what follows you: protections when your laptop dies or your flight gets canceled, solid rewards on everyday spending in any currency and lounges in the airports you actually pass through.

A long list of statement credits might only be great if you'll be back home in a few days. For extended travel, it's more important to pick the card that works wherever you wake up tomorrow.

#6122. The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Will Pay You To Redeem Points Over Peak Dates… But Why?

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is incentivizing people to redeem points at the property for stays over some pretty peak dates, which you don’t often see, as flagged by View from the Wing. This has the potential to be a good deal, but beyond that, I think the more interesting part of this story is the topic of why the hotel would offer something like this, since this is pretty rare.

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points back per night when you redeem over some peak dates, for a total of up to 90,000 points back (which you’d get if redeeming for six nights). To cover the basics:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is a ski-in, ski-out property in Colorado, and it’s one I’ve reviewed before. For what it’s worth, the hotel is currently charging 55,000 World of Hyatt points per night over the dates eligible for this promotion.

Based on my valuation of 1.4 cents per World of Hyatt point, that means a redemption will cost you the equivalent of $770 per night. Meanwhile cash rates are running double as much, and that’s before taxes are factored in.

Understandably, I think a lot of people might be confused as to why the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek would be incentivizing award redemptions in this way. If the hotel wants to fill rooms, why only offer bonus points for points stays, and not for cash stays? That’s especially true when you consider redeeming points is already a good value compared to the cash rate.

The explanation here is probably pretty simple, if you understand the economics at play. I’ve written in the past about how hotels are reimbursed for award stays. Keep in mind that the loyalty program centrally (rather than the individual hotel) sets the cost for redemptions, based on their internal costs associated with redemptions. The way it generally works is as follows:

How does this all factor into the Park Hyatt Beaver Creek’s promotion? I suspect a few factors are at play here:

The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek is offering 15,000 points per night for award redemption over peak holiday dates. So while the standard rate is 55,000 points per night, you’d end up paying 40,000 points per night, which is quite the deal compared to the cash rate.

Given that some hotels treat points guests as second class guests who are staying for “free,” I think the goal here is pretty clear. Hotels are reimbursed for award stays based on overall occupancy levels, and presumably the hotel hopes that a promotion like this will get it to the occupancy level needed to trigger the highest reimbursement rate.

What do you make of this Park Hyatt Beaver Creek promotion?

#6121. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6120. Norse Atlantic Files For Bankruptcy After Lessors Terminate Leases On Its 12 Boeing 787s

Norse Atlantic Airways' Norwegian operating subsidiary is filing for bankruptcy after the airline failed to secure sufficient emergency financing. The announcement came earlier today, just hours after the carrier confirmed that it had received lease termination notices covering all 12 of its Boeing 787 Dreamliners.

The developments follow Thursday's suspension of all flights, bringing an abrupt halt to operations just four and a half years after the airline's launch. Norse had been attempting to reinvent its business, shifting away from its original low-cost transatlantic network towards Asia and flying on behalf of other airlines.

In a stock exchange announcement, Norse confirmed that its Norwegian operating subsidiary would file a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court. However, the listed parent company and its UK subsidiary are not included in the filing, with management continuing to explore opportunities to salvage the remaining business. Norse Atlantic CEO Eivind Roald acknowledged the impact of the decision.

“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners. The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations.”

Norse had appeared to be making progress towards profitability, reducing its annual net loss from $135.5 million in 2024 to $61.9 million in 2025. However, that improvement was dramatically reversed in 2026. Declining income coincided with rising personnel and maintenance costs, while financing expenses were exacerbated by a $32.9 million noncash charge associated with the bond conversion.

Remarkably, Norse's fuel expenditure increased by just 2.5% in the first half of 2026, despite average jet fuel prices soaring by 92% year-on-year in the second quarter. However, beneath the surface, those spiraling costs were still taking their toll.

With no fuel hedging arrangements in place, Norse slashed its own-network capacity by 64% in the quarter, but was unable to reduce its fuel costs, widening its losses. In addition, many of its expenses remained relatively fixed, resulting in substantially higher unit costs and further undermining the economics of its scheduled services.

Norse secured particularly attractive aircraft leases during the pandemic, when demand for widebody aircraft had collapsed. It originally signed agreements with AerCap for nine Dreamliners and BOC Aviation for six more. Having subsequently relinquished its three smaller 787-8s, Norse operates a uniform fleet of 12 Boeing 787-9s. The airline is contesting the validity of the termination notices.

The aircraft could prove particularly desirable to other airlines given the current shortage of modern widebodies and the long wait times as Boeing works through its 787 backlog. LOT Polish Airlines could be a particularly logical candidate, given its existing appetite for secondhand Dreamliners.

The Polish flag carrier has already secured additional aircraft previously operated by Virgin Atlantic. Other existing Rolls-Royce-powered Dreamliner operators could also represent potential destinations. British Airways, which faces delays to its Boeing 777X deliveries, could use additional 787-9s to bolster its long-haul capacity.

Meanwhile, Thai Airways has already turned to secondhand widebodies to support its network expansion. Royal Brunei Airlines, which has ordered four additional Trent 1000-powered 787-9s, could also be a candidate if it seeks to accelerate its fleet growth ahead of those deliveries.

There's potentially another 787 suitor that would surprise everyone: Southwest Airlines, which is reportedly considering adding long-haul flying. Adding 12 Dreamliners within months, rather than waiting in line behind competitors for years, would enable a far more rapid transformation of its business model.

The budget carrier will cease flying to another US airport, which makes seven so far.

Norse launched operations in June 2022 between Oslo and New York, seeking to fill the gap left by Norwegian's withdrawal from long-haul flying. However, the carrier increasingly struggled to make its original business model work. Its attention gradually shifted towards Southeast Asian destinations and aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance contracts with other airlines.

The scale of that transformation is particularly apparent in US Department of Transportation data. Between the summers of 2025 and 2026, Norse reduced its US capacity by more than 60%, including withdrawing all its Los Angeles services. However, its load factors actually improved.

By the time Norse suspended operations on Thursday, London Gatwick–Orlando was its sole remaining scheduled US route. Meanwhile, ACMI and charter flying increased from 11% of Norse's flights in Q2 2025 to 56% in Q2 2026. Such contracts reduced its exposure to fuel prices.

However, they also increased its dependence on individual airline customers. Having lost its six-aircraft IndiGo agreement, Norse secured a smaller deal with Pakistan International Airlines. Ultimately, the carrier recognized the need to reinvent its business but lacked the financial resilience to survive that transformation.

#6119. Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline

Global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency. I’ve had Global Entry for nearly 15 years now. Several weeks ago, I received an email reminding me that I was within six months of my Global Entry expiring, so I just went through the process of renewing it.

In this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically. I’ll include a step-by-step guide, the cost, and the timeline. I’ve separately written about how to apply for Global Entry.

For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities). With this program, approved members can enter the United States using their biometric data at virtually all international airports.

The exact way that biometric data is verified varies by airport. It used to be that you’d have to go up to one of the Global Entry kiosks and answer a few questions. Then they updated the technology, and you just had to stand in front of one of those kiosks for a few seconds. Now many airports just have a camera in the Global Entry lane that automatically verifies your identity as you walk through. It’s pretty awesome.

You do still typically have to walk past an immigration officer and verify that you don’t have anything to declare. You can then proceed to the baggage claim area and exit (unless you’re selected for additional screening).

Over the years, Global Entry has probably saved me dozens of hours. Back in the day I’d be stressed when landing back in the United States, wondering if I’d be stuck in an hour-long immigration queue. Nowadays I can just breeze right through.

Before I share a step-by-step guide of my Global Entry renewal experience, let me share some basics about the timeline, how much it costs, etc.

Global Entry is valid for roughly five years after you’re approved. The reason I say “roughly” is because it’s valid for five years from your next birthday. In other words, if your birthday is December 1, and you apply January 1, 2027, your membership would be valid through December 1, 2032.

If you strategically apply for Global Entry, you can get it for almost six years with one membership. Just apply shortly after your birthday.

Generally speaking you’ll get an email six months before your Global Entry expires informing you of the upcoming expiration. If you want to look for it in your email, that usually comes from [email protected].

Alternatively you can log into your Trusted Traveler Program dashboard, and go to the section that lists your program status. You’ll see the expiration date listed there.

You can apply to have your Global Entry renewed up to a year before the expiration date. There’s no penalty for renewing early, in the sense that it will still be valid for five years from when your membership currently expires, and not five years from when you’re approved. So you might as well renew early.

You won’t want to let your membership lapse, since the process is more complicated for a lapsed membership. Be sure to apply for renewal well before your Global Entry is set to expire.

There is a grace period for Global Entry renewal, as long as you submit your renewal application before your membership expires. Specifically, there’s a grace period of up to 24 months, which is super long. Back in the day, the grace period was only six months, but that has been increased considerably over time.

If you do submit your application but aren’t approved before the expiration, you’ll continue to be able to use Global Entry the same way as before during that period.

It costs $120 for adults to renew Global Entry (Global Entry is free for kids under the age of 18). Fortunately, many credit cards offer a fee credit toward Global Entry renewal. Note that in all cases, you can use your credit for anyone — so if you have extra credits, you can use them for friends and family to renew their Global Entry.

When you first apply for Global Entry you have to be interviewed, either in-person or virtually. Do you need to be interviewed when you renew? It depends:

While only tangentially related, what happens if you have to renew your passport before your Global Entry expires? The good news is that it’s a really easy process.

You just have to log into your account on the Trusted Traveler Programs website and update your passport number there. Your Global Entry will then continue to apply with the new passport up until the Global Entry expiration date. See this post for more details on how that works.

On November 15, 2026, I submitted my application to renew Global Entry. My current membership expires on April 20, 2027, though as long as the application is submitted before then, there’s a grace period of two years.

To renew your Global Entry membership, you’ll want to go to the Trusted Traveler Programs website, and click “LOG IN” at the top right under the “Returning GE/NEXUS/SENTRI/FAST Member/Applicants” heading.

Note that back in 2017 the government migrated from the Global Online Enrollment System (GOES). So if you don’t yet have a new Trusted Traveler Programs profile, you’ll have to set that up first, which is a quick process (though at this point I imagine that virtually everyone has transitioned).

Once logged in you’ll see your current Global Entry membership, and underneath that you should see a “Renew Membership” option listed, assuming you’re within the renewal period.

There you’ll be able to select the program you want to apply for or renew, which in this case would be Global Entry.

Essentially the Global Entry renewal application contains all the information you submitted the last time around, so you just have to confirm that it’s correct, and update any outdated information.

This includes reviewing your personal information, documents, driver’s license, address, employment info, travel history, and more.

You do have to upload a copy of your passport during the process (assuming your passport number changed since your last application, which will likely be the case half of the time for adults, since passports are usually valid for 10 years, while Global Entry is valid for five or so years).

The only slightly complicated part of this process is having to update your travel history, as you have to list all of the countries that you’ve been to since the last time that you applied. So yeah, that can take a second, if you’re a frequent traveler.

At some points the process of reviewing info isn’t very intuitive, as you have to click a lot of unnecessary buttons confirming that nothing has changed. But it’s pretty self explanatory. I’d say the whole process up until this point took me about 15 minutes, and that includes having to recall all the countries from the past five years (which is quite a few).

To finish off the process you just have to certify that all of the information that you’re providing is accurate, and then you have to pay.

When you pay, make sure you use a credit card that has a Global Entry fee credit, assuming you have one.

I used my Amex Business Platinum, and the fee reimbursed within two days.

As mentioned above, I submitted the Global Entry renewal application on November 15, 2026. Then on November 25, 2026 — 10 days later — I received an email indicating that there had been an application status change on the renewal. The email came from [email protected] with the subject line “TTP Application Status Change.”

The email as such doesn’t tell you a whole lot, so you have to log into your account again to see the status. There I found out that the application was approved, meaning that there was no need to take part in an interview.

Experiences seem to be mixed as to whether an interview is required for renewals. For example, during my last renewal, I did need to get an interview, while during my renewal before that, I didn’t need to get an interview.

The good news is that if you do need to be interviewed, you can typically just do so when you return from an international trip. When I did it, it took less than a minute.

I just went through the process of renewing Global Entry, and it was pretty easy. You basically just have to confirm that all the information during your last application is still accurate, add all the countries you’ve been to since then, and pay a fee.

This time around, the application was processed in 10 days, and there was a full approval, so no interview was required. However, don’t be surprised if you do need an interview, as that happened to me during my last renewal.

Hopefully this is useful for anyone else who has a Global Entry renewal coming up soon.

#6117. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

A previous version of this report misstated when Rudy Salas ran for office.

#6116. Here's What Airline Maintenance Technicians Really Earn In 2026

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Airline maintenance technicians are among the best-paid workers in the skilled trades. At several of the largest US airlines, base pay at the top of the scale now passes $60 an hour, before premiums for licenses, shift work, and seniority are added. That puts experienced airline technicians well ahead of the national average for their occupation, which covers repair shops, manufacturers, and smaller operators as well as airlines.

Pay varies widely depending on the employer. Union contracts set rates at most major carriers, Delta sets its own as a non-union airline, and technicians at regional airlines earn considerably less. United’s technicians are still working under an older scale after a new agreement failed to win approval this year. Meanwhile, a long-running shortage of licensed technicians continues to shape what airlines are willing to pay.

Bureau of Labor Statistics data puts the median annual wage for aircraft mechanics and service technicians at $79,870 in May 2025, with a mean annual wage of $84,740 and a median hourly wage of $38.40. The range around that midpoint is wide. The lowest-paid 10% earn less than $48,780 a year, while the top 10% earn more than $128,890. That spread reflects the variety of employers covered, from small general aviation repair shops to the largest airlines.

Where a technician works makes a large difference. Air transportation had a May 2025 median of $96,170 for aircraft mechanics and service technicians, about $16,000 above the national figure for the occupation as a whole. Manufacturing pays less. BLS lists 23,590 aircraft mechanics in aerospace product and parts manufacturing, with a mean hourly wage of $35.84, or $74,550 a year, the industry with the largest single concentration of these jobs. Airlines pay more partly because their technicians work on large transport-category aircraft under union contracts with defined pay scales.

Aircraft technicians also earn well above most other mechanics. BLS puts the median annual wage for automotive service technicians and mechanics at $50,620 in May 2025, which leaves aircraft mechanics about 58% ahead. The difference reflects the training and certification the job requires. Most airline technicians hold an FAA mechanic certificate with airframe and powerplant ratings, which requires an approved training program or documented experience, along with written, oral, and practical exams. National medians also include technicians early in their careers and those outside airlines, so they understate what experienced staff at major carriers earn.

Union contracts set pay at most major US airlines, and they publish it as hourly scales that rise with years of service. At American, technicians represented by the TWU-IAM Association start at $35.59 an hour in their first year and reach a top rate of $60.72 after eight to nine years. That scale is listed as effective January 1, 2026, although the AMT Index, which compiles rates from contract documents, notes that the date has not been confirmed as a payroll start.

Southwest and Alaska, both represented by the Aircraft Mechanics Fraternal Association, sit at almost the same level. Southwest technicians earn $35.77 an hour for their first six months and reach $60.42 after six years, under rates effective August 16, 2026. That is the fastest progression of the three carriers. Alaska’s scale starts at $36.61 an hour at Step 1 and reaches $60.47 at Step 8, with those rates taking effect on October 17, 2026.

The three top rates fall within about 30 cents an hour of one another. At $60.72 an hour, a technician working a standard 2,080-hour year at the top of American’s scale would earn roughly $126,300 in base pay alone. These figures cover base wages only. The AMT Index describes them as scale rates before license, shift, lead, longevity, and retirement add-ons, so most technicians at the top of these scales take home more than the base rate suggests. Years to top pay matters as well, since a shorter progression means a technician reaches the highest rate sooner and earns more over a career.

Why do airlines pay A350 and Boeing 777 Captains the same, even though no US carrier operates both of the aircraft types?

United has the lowest top rate of the four largest US airlines. Its technicians, represented by the Teamsters, start at $29.27 an hour and reach $54.74 after eight years. That scale dates from a contract that became amendable in December 2024. United’s Teamsters-represented technicians began successor-contract talks in August 2024, ahead of the existing agreement’s December 5, 2024, amendable date.

Negotiations produced an agreement in principle in July 2026. The Teamsters said it would deliver industry-leading wage increases, accelerate progression to top pay from eight years to five, and provide a $54 million signing bonus upon ratification, which the union said worked out to $5,000 per member. Pay charts the union published in August said the tentative agreement increases rates by $4.98 or more and reduces basic wage scale progression. Members voted down the agreement in September, so United’s technicians remain on the existing scale while talks continue.

Delta takes a different approach. Its technicians are not represented by a union, so the airline sets pay through company policy and does not publish a full scale. A March 2026 Delta listing for an aircraft maintenance technician in Minneapolis advertised a starting pay of $43.47 per hour, well above the starting rates at American, Alaska, Southwest, and United. Delta also gave employees a raise this year. The airline said it would implement a 4% pay increase for more than 80,000 employees effective June 1, the fifth consecutive year of raises, on top of regular step increases for many frontline teams.

Base scales capture only part of what an airline technician earns. Contracts add premiums for holding an airframe and powerplant certificate, for working line maintenance, and for seniority. The Teamsters’ pay charts for United show how much those additions are worth, defining an all-in rate as basic rates plus a $1.20 VEBA contribution and premiums for A&P, Line, and Longevity. The union estimated that A&P technicians would see pay increases of between $59,342 and $131,747 over the four-year term of the agreement members later rejected. Night shift differentials and overtime come on top of all-in rates.

Pay falls sharply outside the largest carriers. Allegiant technicians start at $36.50 an hour and reach $50.52 after nine years of longevity, and Hawaiian’s scale runs from $30.02 to $47.83 after about eight years. Hawaiian’s rates are also in transition. AMFA won the combined Alaska-Hawaiian representation election on February 25, 2026, and the IAM agreement stays in place until a joint contract is ratified.

Regional airlines pay the least. Horizon technicians reach $39.31 after six years, and PSA’s top rate is $39.00 at nine and 10 years. At Envoy, the agreement’s top step pays $38.51 since November 2025, rising to $39.67 from November 2026. Those top regional rates sit only a few dollars above what a first-year technician earns at American, Alaska, or Southwest.

Airlines are competing for technicians in a tight labor market. Boeing’s 2026 Pilot and Technician Outlook projects that the industry will need about 728,000 new maintenance technicians worldwide over the next 20 years, more than the 674,000 new pilots it expects airlines to require. Boeing describes maintenance technician hiring as one of the most competitive segments of the aviation labor market. Retirements are a major factor. Aviation Week reported that Boeing estimates retirements account for 40% of maintenance technician attrition.

The US training pipeline has grown, but not enough to close the gap. The 2026 Pipeline Report from the Aviation Technician Education Council and Oliver Wyman counted 11,103 new FAA airframe and powerplant mechanic certificates issued in 2025, a record. Even so, Oliver Wyman forecasts demand for 25,000 more North American aviation technical personnel than the industry will have, including 9,100 certificated mechanics. Many newly certificated mechanics also take jobs outside airlines, in general aviation, manufacturing or other industries.

Consultancies outside the industry see the same pressure. McKinsey estimated in March 2026 that without intervention, the technician deficit could reach 60,000 in 2029, and it warned that shortages can drive up aviation costs, delay aircraft turnaround times, and hamper aircraft reliability. Labor costs and maintenance capacity are linked for airlines because a carrier that cannot staff its hangars must send work to outside repair stations or leave aircraft out of service longer. Recent contracts at American, Alaska, and Southwest have pushed top base rates past $60 an hour, while United’s technicians are holding out for terms they consider competitive with those carriers.
