#6115. Amex Blue Business Card Bonus: As High As 50K Points Or $500 Cash Back Welcome Offer

At the moment, we’re seeing increased welcome offers on two of Amex’s most lucrative business cards — The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express and The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card. Ordinarily these cards have really unremarkable bonuses, but at the moment the offers have been improved very nicely — we’re talking doubled on one card, and more than tripled on the other card. If you don’t yet have either card, this is absolutely the time to apply.

I’ll cover the welcome offer on the Amex Blue Business Plus, which I’d argue is one of Amex’s most lucrative and most approachable business cards, especially for those looking to accrue points. I’ll also talk about the Amex Blue Business Cash, which is essentially the cash back version of the card.

Link: Learn more about The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express and The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card

The Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus is currently as high as 50,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of card membership. Apply and find out your welcome offer. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, potentially making this offer worth $850. As a point of comparison, previously the publicly available welcome offer was just 15,000 points after spending $3,000 within the first three months, so this offer is potentially worth more than three times as much. For a no annual fee card (Rates & Fees), this is pretty incredible. This is absolutely the time to apply if you’re interested.

However, as I’ll explain below, the reason you get the card isn’t just because of the welcome offer, but also because of the long term value that it offers. There are lots of great uses of Amex Membership Rewards points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air Canada Aeroplan, to Air France-KLM Flying Club, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give some examples of how points could be redeemed:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a few additional things to note:

Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to generally be among the easiest to get approved for. I also want to emphasize that Amex business cards not counting toward the 5/24 limit really makes the opportunity cost of picking up this card pretty low, for those of us into maximizing our rewards.

The first thing to love about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is that it has no annual fee (Rates & Fees)… you can’t beat that!

But really what makes this card unrivaled within the Amex ecosystem is its return on spending, up to a certain limit. Specifically, the Amex Blue Business Plus offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year, and then 1x points. It’s that straightforward. So $50,000 in spending per year would earn you 100,000 Membership Rewards points.

This is the only no annual fee credit card on the market that earns 2x transferable points that can be moved to the full list of airline and hotel partners at the “premium” ratio. There’s literally not another card like that. The one caveat is that the card does have foreign transaction fees, so I wouldn’t recommend using it for purchases abroad (Rates & Fees).

Speaking of the ability to move points to partners, I think that gets at the other thing that’s awesome about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card — in the event that you want to close other Amex cards (with annual fees) that accrue Membership Rewards points, this is a great card to have, so that you can maintain your points balance, given the ability to pool points.

So I view this as a very low risk card to apply for, especially with it not counting toward Chase’s 5/24 limit. The only reason I wouldn’t get this card is if I’m otherwise at the Amex five credit card limit.

Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Plus Card here.

In the Blue Business portfolio, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is the standout card for me. However, I should also mention the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, which is essentially the cash back equivalent:

Personally, I get more excited by the Amex Blue Business Plus Card than the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, simply because I value Amex points at well over one cent each. That’s why I’d rather earn 2x points rather than 2% cash back. Admittedly, not everyone will feel the same, especially those who don’t actually want to put the effort into maximizing points.

The Amex Blue Business Cash bonus is also greatly improved, though, as it was previously for a $250 statement credit. So this is twice as good.

Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Cash Card here.

The Amex Blue Business Plus Card is a product that often flies under the radar. Ordinarily the card doesn’t have a very exciting bonus, but at the moment, we’re seeing a much better opportunity than usual. The card has a welcome offer as high as 50,000 bonus Membership Rewards points. Getting a no annual fee card that earns 2x transferable points (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1x points) that can be moved directly to airline and hotel partners at the most favorable ratio is something you won’t find on any other card. That’s why this card is in my wallet, and the welcome offer is just the icing on the cake.

Meanwhile if you’re looking for the cash back equivalent, it’s at least worth mentioning the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, which has a bonus as high as $500 cash back as a statement credit. That no annual fee card earns 2% cash back (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1% cash back), also with no annual fee.

These are both really lucrative cards that can be worth holding onto in the long run, so if you’re eligible, I’d absolutely recommend applying.

Anyone else love the Amex Blue Business Plus Card, and think it’s an underrated option in the Amex portfolio?

#6114. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6113. Hyatt Credit Cards Compared: Is The Personal Or Business Card Better?

Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card

To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:

If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

The first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

The annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

The math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

So my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a big spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

That being said, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

What’s your take on the value proposition of Hyatt’s personal vs. business card?

#6112. Alaska Airlines Working With Multiple Agencies To Reduce Law Enforcement After ICE Arrests

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Dozens of airport workers at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) marched to Alaska Airlines headquarters on Tuesday, demanding the carrier call for US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to be removed from the airport. This comes as the employees and airport workers demand greater protection after two passengers were arrested by immigration at the gate last weekend.

Alaska Airlines has confirmed to KING 5 News that it is currently engaging with government authorities and other industry partners for advice on ways to minimize the impact of law enforcement activities on other passengers, employees and general airline operations.

On Saturday, two individuals, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter Sofia Larrondo Hernandez Mejia, were arrested as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight destined for Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). During boarding, ICE officers allegedly pushed past a customer service agent to arrest the two. The customer service agent asked the ICE agent for their credentials before pushing past, and ICE did not notify its own security team before the arrests.

This has raised concerns among employees and other guests, leading demonstrators to gather at Angle Lake Park before marching to the carrier's headquarters. On arrival at the airline's headquarters, they delivered a letter with demands to the airline's management team.

In this letter, the group of union workers and other employees have asked Alaska to publicly call for ICE to be removed from airports, and demand that warrants are required for agents to access the aircraft jet bridges, limit the information shared between airlines and ICE, and protect employees, who, following the recent arrest, feel unsafe at work.

Alaska spoke about the situation in a statement to Simple Flying on Friday.

"Alaska Airlines takes great pride in our long history of running a safe, caring and reliable operation. The safety, dignity and well-being of our guests and employees are fundamental to us, and we believe every traveler should feel safe and respected throughout their journey.

The events of Nov. 21 at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport deeply impacted our employees, guests and community, and we recognize the concerns and questions that have been raised. Our employees are trained to follow Alaska Airlines’ standard procedures and company policies when engaging with federal agencies.

The arrests have affected not only Alaska's workers, but other airlines operatingat the airport as well. A cabin lead at Delta Air Lines, the second-largest operator at SEA, noted that the high-profile arrests have left Nancy Kibocha afraid to return to work. Executive Director of OneAmerica, Washington State's largest immigrant and refugee advocacy organization, Roxana Norouzi, suggested that while airlines are expected to accommodate immigration, carriers do have some power to limit exposure to these arrests for other passengers and crew.

"These longstanding procedures give law enforcement officers, flight crews and airport teams clear, consistent guidance designed to support a safe, orderly environment for employees and guests," the carrier explained. "As an airline, Alaska is required to comply with applicable federal laws and regulations."

In the lead-up to Thanksgiving, this marks one of the busiest travel weekends in the country. Port of Seattle, the operator of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, expects more than one million travelers to pass through the airport this week between Tuesday and Monday. Below is a snapshot of the airport's busiest operators, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics from September 2025 to August.

A pilot reportedly walked off and two flight attendants asked to be replaced after the arrests.

With this demonstration coming on one of the busiest travel weeks of the year, union workers have called on the traveling public to join their demands, which have raised ongoing concerns about airport security procedures and enforcement, despite safety and security protocols being jeopardized.

Alaska confirmed that all its employees receive training and that the company has longstanding procedures for working with federal agencies. The carrier is required to comply with all federal laws and regulations across its network. The Port confirmed that law enforcement officers have broad access across the airport facilities, and the airport cannot interfere with immigration enforcement operations.

Federal agents must have a judicial warrant and other legal authority to access restricted areas of the airport, such as jet bridges, which require access credentials. Alaska has confirmed it will continue to prioritize the safety and well-being of guests and employees.

#6110. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#6109. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

Admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge issues. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

Ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

We arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is currently closed, so we had no lounge option there.

I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

Boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

We boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

These seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

The tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

While the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

So the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an issue. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

Airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

At 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

It was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

The crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

Just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

The lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

The primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

At 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

As we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it shows some effort.

It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

To be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

#6108. 5 Airlines Flying Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 Boeing 787s In 2026, Yet 3 Are Moving New Deliveries To GEnx

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

The Boeing 787 Dreamliner is central to several major airlines’ long-haul fleets, with Rolls-Royce's Trent 1000 serving as one of its two available engine options. However, the relationship between the engine manufacturer and major customers has changed over the years. The biggest fleets are not automatically the biggest believers, as ANA, British Airways and Air New Zealand steer new deliveries toward GE Aerospace’s GEnx.

Meanwhile, LATAM Airlines has returned to the Trent 1000 XE. Examining five 787 operators, namely ANA, Singapore Airlines, British Airways, LATAM and Air New Zealand, reveals how differently airlines are approaching the powerplant behind their Dreamliners. Some are expanding GE-powered fleets, while others are maintaining or renewing their relationship with Rolls-Royce.

As the world's largest operator of the Boeing 787 Dreamliner, according to its own data, All Nippon Airways, based in Japan, maintains a fleet of 90 787s across the 787-8, 787-9 and 787-10 variants. Just over 80 of these aircraft are equipped with Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines.

However, following years of reliability issues with the Trent 1000, ANA has increasingly turned to GE Aerospace's GEnx engines for its newer 787 deliveries, marking a gradual shift away from Rolls-Royce. In 2019, ANA was significantly affected by blade issues within the Trent 1000 engines powering its fleet.

Some blades developed cracks, partly due to vibration under certain operating conditions. In some cases, blades separated from the rotor, potentially resulting in engine failure. Additional engine issues involved corrosion around the blade shanks (the sections attaching the blades to the rotor).

This corrosion led to cracking and the possibility of blades breaking away during operation. These issues affected ANA's 787s equipped with the Trent 1000 Package B and C engines, forcing groundings and repairs at the time, as noted by KN Aviation. Due to the problems ANA experienced with its Trent engines, the airline committed to equipping its future 787s with General Electric's GEnx engine.

On February 25, 2025, the company announced that it would move forward with the GEnx, a proven powerplant that has been in service for more than 15 years. GE states that the engine has accumulated more than 62 million flight hours, with over 3,000 units in service and on order, including spare units. The GEnx also powers two-thirds of all 787 aircraft currently in operation.

The Hong Kong carrier will become the only oneworld member flying out of the new terminal, using a lounge to create its custom premium experience.

Singapore Airlines has the unique distinction of being the first airline to operate the 787-10. According to Options, the airline officially received its first 787-10 on March 25, 2018. The aircraft began its inaugural flight from Boeing's South Carolina plant, located in North Charleston, near Charleston International Airport (CHS). After 22 hours, the aircraft landed in Singapore via Osaka.

That initial delivery was the first of a planned fleet of 49 Dreamliners. Fast-forward eight years, and according to Planespotters.net, Singapore Airlines currently has 26 of the aircraft in active service and two parked, for a total of 28 787s. Given that each Dreamliner is powered by two Trent 1000 engines, the airline maintains 56 units of the Rolls-Royce powerplant across its current fleet.

Singapore Airlines primarily introduced the 787-10 for regional and medium-haul operations, with the aircraft configured to accommodate 337 passengers across two classes. The airline initially deployed the Dreamliner on routes to Osaka and Perth, demonstrating its role in serving high-demand regional markets.

Much like ANA, British Airways operates all three 787 variants: the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10. The airline maintains 12 787-8s, 18 787-9s, and 12 787-10s, giving it a total fleet of 42 Dreamliners, according to company sources. While the Trent 1000 had enjoyed several years as the primary engine of BA's 787 fleet, the London fog began to obscure the partnership two years ago.

In 2024, the airline selected GE's GEnx-1B engine for six of its incoming 787s rather than maintain its course with Rolls-Royce and its Trent 1000 engines. At the time, BA CEO and Chairman Sean Doyle told Aviation Week that "we ran a competition this time around, and we factored in cost and quality, your total cost of maintenance, and that's been the driver of our decision."

The decision marked a significant shift in British Airways' long-standing relationship with Rolls-Royce, with the airline increasingly turning to the American manufacturer for its future Dreamliner deliveries. In terms of future orders, London South East states that the airline currently has 32 787-10s on order, all of which will be powered by GE engines. This represents a gut punch for Rolls-Royce and signals a significant shift in BA's confidence in the two manufacturers.

Of this large order, two aircraft have very recently been delivered. One joined the company on October 14, and another followed closely on November 7. With two of the new GE-powered Dreamliners already delivered, British Airways is beginning to put that transition into practice, leaving Rolls-Royce with a shrinking role in the airline's future 787 fleet.

LATAM has a fleet of around 400 aircraft, as reported by ALN News. Providing a large portion of the airline's passenger capacity is its 787 fleet, which currently consists of 41 aircraft. By 2028, LATAM plans to increase that number to 48, according to its 2026 third-quarter report.

Like many companies making the switch, in 2023 GE noted that LATAM had decided to equip its next 787 deliveries with GEnx engines. AeroTime reports that the 2023 order consisted of 16 787-9s, with LATAM choosing the GEnx due to long-running issues with the Trent 1000 Package C engines that equipped a portion of its 787 fleet.

However, all is not lost regarding Rolls-Royce's foothold in the Latin American market. AeroTime states that the engine manufacturer announced that LATAM has once again selected its upgraded Trent 1000 XE engine. The selection provides Rolls-Royce with a customer win that it can point to as it seeks to rebuild confidence in its engines amid concerns among global carriers operating the 787 family.

The selection also signals a renewed commitment to Rolls-Royce, particularly as LATAM looks to expand its long-haul network and strengthen the efficiency of its existing Dreamliner fleet. Regarding the selection, LATAM CEO Roberto Alvo stated that:

“The incorporation of the Trent 1000 XE on our Boeing 787 aircraft supports our efforts to enhance operational efficiency, while providing optionality to capture growth opportunities as we continue developing our long-haul network,”

The jets will be delivered in the early to mid-2030s.

The carrier in this list with the smallest number of 787s is Air New Zealand, which currently operates 14 of the aircraft, with an additional 10 on order, according to the airline's website. Like other airlines operating the 787, the carrier experienced similar troubles with the Trent 1000. In 2019, the company selected the GEnx engine to power eight of its future 787-10s, with the possibility of increasing that number to 20, according to GE.

That firm order was valued at more than $480 million (£367 million) at list prices, and deliveries of the GEnx-powered aircraft began in 2022. The Trent 1000 problems had a major impact on the company's operations, with five of its 14 Boeing 787-9s grounded and unavailable at the height of the disruption.

The airline described the engine shortage as one of the most significant supply chain challenges facing aviation, and aircraft shortages affected its finances and ability to operate its long-haul network. According to AeroTime, the final stored Dreamliner returned to Auckland (AKL) in June 2026. The aircraft resumed commercial flying two days later, marking an important step toward restoring availability across the carrier's existing widebody fleet.

The return followed extensive maintenance and engine work. Air New Zealand is now getting ready to grow its Dreamliner fleet with a second engine type. Its 10 incoming aircraft comprise five 787-9s and five 787-10s, all powered by GE Aerospace GEnx-1B engines, rather than Rolls-Royce Trent 1000s. Ch-aviation reported that manufacturing delays pushed the first new 787-9 deliveries into 2027.

Meanwhile, Fleet Wire says two new aircraft joined the fleet in October 2026. Operating both engine types will require separate spare engines and support arrangements, adding another consideration as the airline expands its Dreamliner operations, including services to Houston, Vancouver, Shanghai and Taipei as aircraft arrive across its network.

#6106. Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

In the spirit of trying out new ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.

I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could. This is not a full review — rather, it’s some general comments on the seats, food, and tech, in Air France’s economy offering.

After completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes. Yes, including La Première – I do fly in the pointy end sometimes. 😉

Having transited through Paris Charles de Gaulle so many times now, I’m actually starting to learn my way around the crazy maze of terminals.

On this occasion, the transfer was on the simpler side, as both flights used gates in Terminal 2E. That said, I still had to catch the light rail transit from Hall K to Hall L and pass through a full security screening before entering the departures area. Not all airports in Europe require this, and I hope it’s taken into account when CDG simplifies its terminal numbering, which is expected in March 2027.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I had access to Air France’s Hall L Lounge, which is currently undergoing some refurbishments.

Getting a post- or pre-flight facial would have been amazing, but, like my five previous visits to Air France’s lounges in Paris, I’ve had no luck at getting a slot.

Either there were simply no slots left, or, as on this visit, the remaining slot(s) were after my departure time.

Speaking of lounges, I took this photo from Air France’s lounge in Terminal 2E, Hall K, on a previous trip. According to a staffer I spoke with, the construction outside will eventually be a huge new flagship Air France lounge for Terminal 2E.

I sent this photo to Ben before I boarded, and he was surprised to see that the board specifically referenced pre-boarding for Flying Blue Ultimate members. In case you didn’t know either, now you do.

Here’s one final pic for the AvGeeks: even though Air France’s version of the A380 wasn’t particularly loved, the elevated jetbridge above the Boeing 777-300ER in this pic was a nostalgic reminder of the airline’s former superjumbos.

If you’re locking in for 10+ hour flight in economy, there’s only a limited level of comfort that any airline would be able to offer. I wasn’t envious at all walking through the premium economy cabin during boarding…

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I was able to choose any seat in the cabin from 72 hours before departure. Contrary to my avoidance of bulkhead/exit row seats and their fixed armrests on night flights, I picked bulkhead window seat 21L in the front row of the economy cabin.

The legroom here was more than I needed for this day flight. My plan was to spend most of the flight working, so this seat also avoided anyone reclining into my laptop.

Of Air France’s three Airbus A350-900 configurations, this was the newest 292-seater version that has been rolling out since 2023. The economy cabin has 212 seats in a 3-3-3 layout, which I know isn’t usually a favorite of families of four. Non-bulkhead/exit row seats have a pitch of around 31 inches.

I didn’t move the four-way adjustable headrest at all during the flight, and the recline is listed as being around 118 degrees.

No matter where I’m sitting, I can’t help but marvel at that wingtip.

Of the 29 flights I’ve taken with Air France, I can only remember one meal that wasn’t good. In fact, it was terrible, and was actually when I was flying premium economy from Paris to Zanzibar (ZNZ) in 2024.

Of the two meal choices, I went for the chicken pasta (I didn’t note down the second option as I only decided to write about this after the flight).

I thoroughly enjoyed the main dish. It had lots of protein, the sauce was flavorful, and the little mini pasta pieces weren’t dry at all. Given the several accompaniments, I consider this a generous helping of food. The Président camembert cheese was a nice premium touch, and the bread roll was quite the opposite of stale. I can’t tell you how good the mini apple tart was, as I’m intolerant to apples.

I wish there had been a menu so I could know for sure what was in this really tasty salad. I’m pretty sure it was a mix of mainly carrots, potato, and barley, in what I guess was a honey mustard sauce.

For those who don’t know, Air France differentiates itself by serving Champagne in economy. Partial though I can be, I stuck to Coke Zero for the caffeine.

I like the intention of using wood instead of plastic for cutlery; I just wish the knife could actually cut!

Despite the hefty lunch serving, I got very hungry midway through the flight as I didn’t eat a proper breakfast. I went to raid the snack baskets at the rear-most galley. The area very busy with lots of passengers lingering, and there was some kerfuffle over a medical issue, so I didn’t take any pictures.

I did, however, get a snap of my snack haul. A mini ice cream, a couple of chocolate truffles, a packet of savory biscuits, and half a cheese sandwich. While the snacks might have lacked in nutrition, it’s nice to know that you won’t go hungry on Air France’s economy flights.

I was so tired after the 3:30 a.m. alarm that I skipped the pre-landing light meal on the return flight in favor of a nap.

Neither did I touch the box containing a very beige selection of a bread roll and a pastry on the flight to Paris from Rio. Craving caffeine after a patchy night of sleep, I attempted the drip-style coffee, but a sip was enough to turn my nose up. Yes, I am a coffee snob, and I’m proud of it.

Air France made a great choice to mount the IFE screens on the bulkhead. Only the screen in the aisle seat in my row of three was in that annoying underseat position that needs to be folded away for takeoff and landing.

I could just about reach the very tactile screen when leaning forward. Otherwise, there was a mousepad-style remote.

The 13.3-inch screens are among the largest in the industry, and are the same size as those in the premium economy cabin on this plane.

I counted four charging outlets: a USB-C and a USB-A port in the IFE screen, and, under the seat, a regular power outlet and a second USB-C port.

As for Wi-Fi connectivity, there were no disruptions to the complimentary Starlink for the duration of the flight. However, the whole IFE system had to be reset shortly after we took off. Then, a few hours into the flight, the vast majority of the movies disappeared from the system, including the one I was halfway through. I was able to connect my AirPods to the screen with no issue.

Other amenities, so to speak, were a rather coarse pillow, a blanket, and over-the-head headphones.

One of my favorite things about flying and traveling is meeting new people, including cabin crew, though due to the busyness of economy cabins, that can be tough.

If I have time, I also try to bring a sweet treat on board for the crew to enjoy during the flight, no matter which cabin I’m flying in, as it is usually a great way to build rapport. It worked on this flight, as several crew members came to thank me for the mince pies. Mattieu, to whom I handed them during boarding, brought me a little note to say thanks for both the pies and my Flying Blue loyalty.

Over the course of the flight, I noticed crew in the economy cabin engaging enthusiastically with passengers. At the start of interactions during meal service, I even heard crew asking passengers whether their preferred language was English or French. On at least three occasions, I noticed crew walking through the cabin offering water.

After being spoiled with lots of lie-flat beds over the years, I’ll admit the pre-flight excitement isn’t quite the same when boarding a long-haul flight in economy. This return trip in Air France economy was perfectly fine, with the pros certainly outweighing the cons.

Whether you only fly business class, or a frequent economy class flier, I hope you gained some insights into the Air France economy experience.

When was the last time you flew long-haul in economy, and how was the experience?

#6105. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

#6103. Delta Air Lines Teases Routes For 20 New A350-1000s: Where They Could Fly

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

SkyTeam Alliance partner Delta Air Lines is expecting 20 of Airbus's largest single-level widebody aircraft. The Airbus A350-1000 is a firm order with 20 options, and deliveries are expected to begin in 2027. With these planes set to help support the airline's long-haul ambitions, the airline has already hinted that the next decade could see the airline push further west.

In a report shared by Executive Traveller, Delta is gearing up for the 'decade of the Pacific', suggesting the airline will look to expand its reach to destinations in Asia and Oceania. Australia is likely to be the biggest winner here.

Delta is one of three of the US legacy carriers, all of which have growing networks to both Asia and Oceania. Delta itself has grown capacity in these regions by 15% year-on-year since 2022. The airline's Seoul-based Vice President for the Asia Pacific, Jeff Moomaw, noted that this could be just the beginning.

The majority of the airline's future expansion in the next decade is expected to be westward, and this could see the carrier expand to other destinations around the Pacific Rim. All of Delta's current flights to Australia operate from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), where the airline is the largest carrier with more than 200 daily departures to 70 cities.

Seattle remains the airline's second-largest gateway on the US West Coast, with its northern geography providing better connectivity to Southeast Asian markets. Currently, the airline serves nonstop routes to Seoul, Shanghai, and Taipei. Tokyo will join in March. Year-round and seasonal destinations include:

A nonstop service from the US to Singapore remains a priority for Delta; however, it remains to be seen which aircraft type the airline will deploy on the route. Competitor United Airlines already serves Singapore nonstop from San Francisco (SFO), while Singapore Airlines maintains several services to the US from its hub at Singapore Changi (SIN).

Hong Kong has returned to the airline network from Los Angeles after close to eight years of suspension. This joined Taipei (TPE) and Shanghai (PVG), with Manila planning to begin in March. The carrier already maintains seasonal services to Auckland (AKL) and Brisbane (BNE), operating across the Northern Hemisphere winter season, where less demand is required for the airline's widebodies for flights to Europe. This sees most North American carriers redeploy aircraft to warmer temperatures south.

The majority of Delta's South Pacific network is concentrated at Los Angeles, and after the airport's multibillion-dollar redevelopment program, it makes clear sense for the airline to consider its network expansion from this airport. Services to Sydney (SYD) and Melbourne (MEL), which already receive the A350-900, could be upgraded to the larger A350-1000 once these come online.

SkyTeam ties and hub synergy hint at smoother connections and expanded long haul reach via Incheon gateways.

Delta can utilize the ultra-long-range capabilities and high passenger capacity to operate transpacific routes to Australia and Asia, where smaller planes could potentially not reach. Delta will likely use the first lot of the new plane for long-haul destinations that have continually provided consistent payloads that are otherwise reaching the limit of the A350-900.

The airline already plans to configure the new aircraft with its highest share of premium seats seen across its fleet, with next-generation Delta One suites and an expansion to its Premium Select seating. These include suites with sliding doors, longer lie-flat beds, and larger onboard entertainment screens, which should attract long-haul business or leisure demand.

With the delivery of the A350-1000 expected in 2027, this will become the largest aircraft in the Delta fleet since the Boeing 747, and while any new destination is yet to be confirmed, the airline has explained that as more deliveries arrive, it is highly likely that these will be seen across the Pacific.

#6102. Traveler Says American Pilots Should Have Just “Had A Cup Of Coffee” Instead Of Following Federal Law

There’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong. Furthermore, not everyone is a frequent traveler, and understands the ins and outs of how the airline industry functions.

So that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger. The complaint is so incredibly off base in the first place. But what’s even worse is that when this person is confronted with reality, he just doubles down and keeps going. This person deserves to be roasted, and if you ask me, should be banned from the airline.

Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:

I won’t be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn’t drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir

I won't be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn't drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/q1I8pjsM3w

I can totally appreciate how frustrating it is when a flight is canceled, but this is actually very simple — federal regulations dictate the maximum number of hours that pilots can fly, and that’s for good reason. The airline industry operates with the goal of putting safety above all else, and pilot fatigue has been a contributing factor to many accidents over the years.

I totally get it, you want to be home for Thanksgiving, and it sucks things went wrong, but those are the facts. This is federal law, and on top of that, we should want pilots to be well rested, rather than just saying “keep working, just have another cup of coffee.”

I’d like to point out what makes this even worse — this was a flight out of Miami last night, and the airport had shut down due to a ground stop, because a FedEx MD-11 ran off the runway. That was an absolute pain for all passengers out of the airport, and I can assure you that American also wasn’t happy about that happening, and the impact it had on its operations.

All would be forgiven if this traveler either just didn’t say anything further, or acknowledged “ah, I wasn’t aware of that.” Instead, he has had dozens and dozens of posts, just going on and on and on.

He posted about how American claimed the cancelation was the airport’s fault, but insisted “it’s actually these pilots fault,” and suggested “pilots will lie to save money for their company.”

@AmericanAir will cancel your flight the day before Thanksgiving and say it's the airports fault. It's actually these pilots fault. pic.twitter.com/v4t8KPSojR

@AmericanAir pilots will lie to save money for their company @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/7VmOKILwCL

He then attacked American’s rebooking lines at Miami Airport. Look, I’ll be the first to call out American when they fall short (and they often do!), but if you really can’t figure out why rebooking lines “wrap around the corner” on one of the busiest travel days of the year when there was an accident that shut down an airport, then you really aren’t trying very hard to understand things.

@AmericanAir why do your rebooking lines always wrap around the corner? How bad are your operations? pic.twitter.com/Id8AaTiom1

He also has an issue with bathrooms at Miami Airport, which I get, but goodness, he’s repetitive.

Why do you have the most disgusting bathrooms @iflymia

Why are your bathroom never clean@iflymia

Why are your bathrooms such a health hazard @iflymia

You should hire people to clean your bathrooms@iflymia

He then suggested that he’ll fly Delta or United next time, because they can get you where you’re supposed to go. Yeah, sure bro, they’ll get you out of Miami Airport when it’s closed due to an accident.

Next time I'll fly @united or @Delta because they can actually get you where you are supposed to be when you are supposed to be there…and paid for…unlike the incompetent airline @AmericanAir. I bet your life is full of incompetence

He’s also asking Secretary Duffy to investigate American, because “they are the most unethical and corrupt company in America.” We know the Trump administration loves to investigate corruption, I’m sure they’ll get right on that!

Can you investigate @AmericanAir they are the most unethical and corrupt company in America

Honestly, I think American is perfectly justified in banning this guy. He’s violating the company’s policy on photographing employees, and this kind of behavior doesn’t need to be tolerated.

It sucks when things go wrong while flying, especially for travel around the holidays. But there’s a fine line between a reasonable complaint, and one that’s completely uncalled for. Posting pictures of random pilots and suggesting they’re the reason you can’t see your family for Thanksgiving is not acceptable.

What’s even worse is when people explain that crew rest requirements are federally mandated, but you just remain in denial over that, and double down. American, please do everyone else a favor and ban this guy.

#6101. Kimpton Social Password Winter 2026-2027: “This Calls For Something”

Kimpton has a pretty cool “social password” concept, whereby you can receive extra perks for sharing a phrase at check-in. Kimpton generally has this promotion a couple of times per year — we last saw this in summer, and there’s now a new password for winter.

I’d like to talk about what the new password is, share my experience using it, and also pose a question to Kimpton regulars about the least cringeworthy way to go about saying it.

Kimpton is one of the cooler IHG hotel groups, and there are a variety of things that set Kimpton apart from other IHG brands. One of those things is the social password. The idea is that seasonally, Kimpton provides a phrase through social media that you’re supposed to say when you check-in, and if you do that, you’ll receive something extra.

The new Kimpton password is “this calls for something,” and it’s valid for stays between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027. So just say that when you check-in at a Kimpton property during the promotion period, and you’ll receive a surprise.

For those curious about what happens when you say the Kimpton password, I stayed at the Kimpton EPIC Miami some time back, which was my first Kimpton stay in quite a while (and I haven’t stayed at one since either). It was a good value as well, as I was able to use a free night award earned with the New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more).

I was curious what the benefit would be for using the password. So I shared the password with the front desk agent. At the conclusion of the check-in experience, he brought out a game show-style wheel. I might have spun too hard, as it must have gone around for about 30 seconds. Go figure I landed on the tile that just had me spin again.

Then I spun again, and the prize was free parking. I had a car and was staying for two nights, and parking costs $44 per night. So using the Kimpton password saved me nearly $100 — score!!

Based on looking at the wheel, it seems that some of the other prizes include a free welcome drink, free breakfast, free snacks, and a free movie. There were also a few empty squares, where I guess you don’t win anything. And I’m not sure what the alarm clock, car tipping over, or postcard of Miami get you. Regardless, I’d say those are some awesome prizes, and I got a great reward.

It’s cute how the Kimpton EPIC Miami makes a game of this. I know there’s a lot of inconsistency when it comes to this benefit across Kimpton properties. Some hotels provide meaningful perks (an upgrade, free, parking, etc.), like I got here, while other hotels provide a 19 cent branded koozie.

It’s great that this has stuck around, given that it has presumably become increasingly popular. Years ago not everyone was on social media, so it was a good way to encourage people to follow Kimpton on X, Facebook, Instagram, etc. With the way the internet has evolved, times have changed a bit.

I’m sure I’m not the only one who finds the concept of saying a password at check-in to be kind of weird. So I think it’s fun to compare notes about how people share the password at the front desk. I find it awkward to just blurt out the password out of nowhere.

So when I used this for my stay, I said “I guess I’m supposed to say [social password] as the social password?” That did the trick, but I’d be curious to hear how other Kimpton regulars go about this!

Between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027, Kimpton’s social password is “this calls for something.” Just state that phrase when you check-in at a Kimpton, and you should get some sort of a surprise. The gift will vary by property, so there’s no reason not to take advantage of this if staying at a Kimpton.

The last time I used the password I got to spin a wheel at check-in, and then I ended up getting free parking, which was a value of $44 per night.

If you’ve used the Kimpton password, what was your experience like?
