#6098. The Engineering Tricks Boeing Had To Come Up With To Fit Bigger Fans Under A 1960s Wing

During the 1960s, Boeing introduced several aircraft that would transform commercial aviation, including the 727, 737, and 747. The Boeing 737, which made its first flight in April 1967, was designed for short-haul operations and would eventually become one of the best-selling commercial aircraft families in aviation history.

The original 737 was designed around relatively small, narrow engines. However, as engine technology advanced, Boeing faced the challenge of fitting increasingly larger and more efficient engines beneath wings positioned unusually close to the ground. Rather than addressing this limitation through a single redesign, Boeing introduced a series of engineering modifications across successive 737 generations, culminating in the 737 MAX. So, what changes did Boeing make to accommodate these larger engines, and what compromises did they involve?

The 1960s marked a period of significant expansion for Boeing, with the manufacturer introducing several aircraft that would transform commercial aviation. After introducing the four-engine Boeing 707 in 1958 and the three-engine 727 in 1962, Boeing developed the twin-engine 737 to serve the growing short-haul market. The first 737 took flight on April 9, 1967, seating approximately 100 passengers and offering a range of around 2,500 miles (4,023 km).

The original 737 was designed to operate efficiently at airports with limited ground-handling infrastructure. One of the most significant decisions during its development was Boeing engineer Joseph Sutter's proposal to mount the engines beneath the wings rather than on the rear fuselage, as seen on competing aircraft. This arrangement helped define the 737's distinctive design, while its low fuselage allowed ground crews to access baggage compartments and service the aircraft without specialized lifting equipment. This configuration was well suited to the relatively narrow Pratt & Whitney JT8D engines. However, as engine technology advanced, manufacturers increasingly adopted high-bypass turbofans, which improve propulsive efficiency by moving larger volumes of air around the engine core. Their larger fans, however, require considerably more space beneath the wing.

This became a challenge when Boeing developed the 737 Classic family, beginning with the 737-300. The manufacturer selected the larger CFM56-3 high-bypass turbofan to replace the original JT8D engines, but the aircraft's low wing position and short landing gear left insufficient space for a conventional installation. Boeing therefore had to find a way to accommodate the larger engines while maintaining adequate ground clearance.

By the early 1980s, advances in engine technology prompted Boeing to select the CFM56-3 for its new 737 Classic family, replacing the original low-bypass Pratt & Whitney JT8D with a larger, more fuel-efficient high-bypass turbofan. The engine's fan diameter increased from approximately 40 inches (102 cm) to 60 inches (152 cm), while the aircraft retained its original low-slung architecture. The CFM56-3 offered improved fuel efficiency and lower noise levels, with fuel consumption improvements of approximately 20% compared with the JT8D. However, its larger diameter meant Boeing could not simply replace the existing engines without modifying their installation.

Working with CFM International, Boeing adapted the CFM56-3 to fit beneath the 737 Classic's low wings. The engine nacelle (the outer casing surrounding the engine) received a distinctive flattened lower profile to maintain sufficient ground clearance. To achieve this, components such as the accessory gearbox were relocated from beneath the engine to its sides. The resulting shape, sometimes nicknamed the "hamster pouch," became one of the 737 Classic's most recognizable features. This engineering compromise allowed Boeing to accommodate the larger engine without undertaking an extensive redesign of the aircraft's landing gear and basic airframe architecture. The table below illustrates the timeline of engine installations across successive Boeing 737 generations, which will be explored throughout this article. For a closer look at the CFM56-3's design, Laura Laster provides a detailed explanation in A Boeing 737 Engine CFM56-3 Quick Overview.

Flattened nacelle and relocated accessories

Larger engine with further installation changes

However, modifying the nacelle's shape alone was not enough to overcome the 737's ground clearance limitations. Boeing also had to reconsider how the engines were positioned relative to the wings, introducing another engineering solution that would continue to evolve across subsequent generations.

The popular narrowbody has been a familiar sight in the skies for decades.

Nearly a decade after introducing the 737 Classic, Boeing launched the 737 Next Generation (NG) program in November 1993. Designed to compete directly with the Airbus A320 family, the NG represented one of the most extensive upgrades to the 737, introducing a redesigned wing, strengthened landing gear, and improved performance while retaining the aircraft's basic architecture. The new wing featured a greater span of approximately 117 feet, 5 inches (35.79 meters), increased fuel capacity, and improved aerodynamic efficiency, helping extend the aircraft's range and raise its operating ceiling to 41,000 feet (12,497 meters).

The 737 NG also introduced the CFM56-7B engine, featuring a fan diameter of approximately 61 inches (155 cm), slightly larger than the Classic's CFM56-3. To accommodate larger engines beneath the 737's lower wings, Boeing continued refining an approach first introduced with the Classic: mounting the engines farther forward and higher relative to the wing. This positioned the fan section ahead of the wing's leading edge rather than directly underneath it, helping maintain sufficient ground clearance. The CFM56-7B also delivered approximately 7% better fuel efficiency than its predecessor, along with improved climb performance and reduced noise levels.

However, the next generation of high-bypass turbofans required even larger fans to achieve further efficiency improvements. When Boeing began developing the 737 MAX, the aircraft's low wing position and relatively short landing gear once again limited the size of the engines it could accommodate. With the new CFM LEAP engine offering a substantial increase in fan diameter, Boeing faced another challenge: how could it install a larger, more efficient engine without fundamentally redesigning the 737?

Fast-forward to 2011, when Boeing launched the 737 MAX program as the successor to the 737 Next Generation family. The new aircraft would be powered exclusively by the CFM International LEAP-1B, a next-generation high-bypass turbofan developed to deliver greater fuel efficiency and lower emissions. The LEAP family introduced several advanced technologies, including 3D-woven carbon fiber composite fan blades and improved thermal efficiency. According to CFM International, the engines deliver approximately 15% lower fuel consumption and CO₂ emissions compared with previous-generation engines. However, Boeing's decision to retain the 737's low-slung architecture meant that the LEAP-1B had to be adapted to fit the aircraft's limited ground clearance.

Unlike the LEAP-1A, which powers the Airbus A320neo and features a 78-inch (198 cm) fan, the 737 MAX's LEAP-1B was designed with a smaller fan measuring approximately 69.4 inches (176 cm) in diameter. This nearly nine-inch (23 cm) difference was largely driven by the 737's shorter landing gear and lower wing position. The smaller fan also contributed to a lower bypass ratio of approximately 9:1, compared with around 11:1 for the LEAP-1A. Although a higher bypass ratio can improve propulsive efficiency, the LEAP-1B's design allowed Boeing to benefit from newer engine technology without fundamentally redesigning the 737's airframe.

Despite the smaller fan, the LEAP-1B was still considerably larger than the CFM56-7B used on the 737 NG, which had a fan diameter of approximately 61 inches (155 cm). The increase of more than eight inches (20 cm) meant that reducing the LEAP's fan diameter alone was insufficient to solve the aircraft's ground clearance limitations. Boeing therefore needed to introduce further modifications to the 737 MAX's engine installation and landing gear, raising another question: how could the manufacturer accommodate the larger engines while preserving the aircraft's existing design?

The HPT durability kit has just been certified and promises to deal with extreme conditions issues suffered by the LEAP engine family.

The Boeing 737 MAX was designed exclusively around the CFM International LEAP-1B engine, allowing Boeing to focus on integrating a single engine type into the existing 737 architecture. However, even with its smaller fan diameter, the LEAP-1B required additional ground clearance. To accommodate the larger engines, Boeing extended the MAX's nose landing gear by approximately eight inches (20 cm), raising the front of the aircraft. This modification was possible because the nose landing gear bay offered more vertical space than the main landing gear bays, making it a more practical solution than substantially redesigning the aircraft's undercarriage.

Boeing also repositioned the LEAP-1B engines farther forward and higher relative to the wing than on the 737 NG. Combined with the longer nose landing gear and a revised nacelle design, these modifications provided sufficient ground clearance while preserving much of the 737's original architecture. However, the larger, repositioned engines also affected the aircraft's aerodynamic characteristics, particularly at elevated angles of attack. To address differences in handling characteristics, Boeing introduced the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS), designed to automatically command nose-down stabilizer trim under certain flight conditions.

Although these modifications helped Boeing develop a more fuel-efficient competitor to the Airbus A320neo while maintaining commonality with earlier 737 models, the MCAS system subsequently became central to one of the most serious crises in Boeing's history. Investigations into the crashes of Lion Air Flight 610 in October 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in March 2019, which killed a combined 346 people, identified serious flaws in pilot training. The accidents ultimately led to the worldwide grounding of the 737 MAX and extensive changes to its flight control systems.

Boeing's decision to retain the 737's basic architecture allowed it to introduce more efficient engines without developing an entirely new aircraft. However, the design required several compromises, including the LEAP-1B's smaller fan, revised engine mounting, and landing gear modifications. While these changes helped Boeing remain competitive with the Airbus A320neo, the long-term consequences of adapting an aircraft originally designed in the 1960s have proved far more difficult to quantify.

The financial and reputational costs of the 737 MAX crisis have extended well beyond the aircraft itself. The two fatal accidents, subsequent worldwide grounding, compensation payments, legal proceedings, and production disruptions have cost Boeing tens of billions of dollars. The crisis also intensified scrutiny of Boeing's engineering and certification practices, contributing to a more demanding regulatory environment. The 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 have faced prolonged certification delays, while the separate 777X program has also experienced years of setbacks and extensive regulatory oversight. Meanwhile, Airbus has strengthened its position in the commercial aircraft market, increasing the competitive pressure on Boeing.

Developing an entirely new aircraft rather than continuing to modify the 737 might appear to have been a better long-term decision. However, the challenges extend beyond the MAX. Future improvements in propulsion technology could require significantly larger fans or entirely different engine architectures, potentially exceeding the limits of the 737's existing configuration. CFM International's Revolutionary Innovation for Sustainable Engines (RISE) program, for example, is developing open-fan technology targeting the next generation of commercial aircraft, with the potential for substantial fuel-efficiency improvements. As Boeing looks to its next generation of narrowbody aircraft, will further modifications suffice, or is an entirely new design necessary?

#6097. Buy American AAdvantage Miles For 50% Off (1.88 Cents Each): Worth It?

American Airlines is currently offering a rare elevated promotion on purchasing AAdvantage miles. Through December 2, 2026, AAdvantage members can purchase miles with up to a 50% discount, which is potentially an opportunity to buy miles for 1.88 cents each.

While that’s not a price at which I’d proactively pick up miles, there are definitely some situations where that could represent a good value, if you have an immediate use in mind, especially for first and business class travel.

Note that offers like this are extremely rare — while American offers a 40% off promotion on buying miles consistently, the 50% off promotion seems to come around just once or twice per year.

Link: Buy American Airlines AAdvantage miles with a discount

Between 12:01AM CT on November 27 and 11:59PM CT on December 2, 2026, American AAdvantage is offering up to a 50% discount (or 100% bonus, if you prefer) on buying miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger discount the more miles you buy, as follows:

As you can see, you need to buy a lot of miles to get the best price!

Ordinarily American sells AAdvantage miles for 3.5 cents each pre-tax, or 3.76 cents after factoring in the 7.5% federal excise tax. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. In this case if you max out the promotion and buy 500,000 AAdvantage miles, you’d pay a total of $9,406.25, which comes out to 1.88 cents per mile (that factors in the 7.5% tax).

Keep in mind that American Airlines mileage purchases are non-refundable, and buying AAdvantage miles doesn’t count toward your Loyalty Points total (other than any amount you may spend on an eligible credit card). Purchased miles typically post nearly instantly, but in some cases, it can take up to four hours for them to post.

The 50% discount is the best price we’ve seen from American AAdvantage in recent years, and again, it only comes around once or twice per year. With the standard 40% off promotion on buying miles, you’d ordinarily pay 2.26 cents per mile.

The American AAdvantage program ordinarily allows members to buy at most 300,000 miles per account per calendar year, before factoring in any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 500,000 miles. AAdvantage accounts less than 30 days old aren’t eligible to buy American Airlines miles. Miles can only be purchased in 1,000-point increments.

The process of buying American Airlines miles is easy — the easiest way is to simply follow this link. Alternatively, you can go to aa.com, click on “AAdvantage” at the top of the page, and then click on “Buy, gift or transfer miles.”

From there, you’ll be prompted to log into your AAdvantage account, and then that’s where you can select how many miles you’d like to buy. When you buy American Airlines miles, they’ll typically post to your account instantly.

Yes, you absolutely can buy American Airlines miles, you just have to be aware of a few restrictions. For one, your account needs to be at least 30 days old. On top of that, you have to stay within the annual cap.

It’s possible to buy miles for yourself or others, but you’ll need to be sure you use the right account to make the purchase.

Here’s every promotion on purchased AAdvantage miles we’ve tracked since November 2025, with the cost per mile for each, so you can see how the current deal stacks up.

Is this a good deal? At 1.88 cents per mile, the current promotion is 50% below the standard price. That matches the best deal we’ve tracked. It’s 0.38 cents above our 1.5-cent valuation of AAdvantage miles.

Cost per mile at the largest purchase tier, including the 7.5% tax. Lower is better.

Every American Airlines AAdvantage miles purchase promotion since November 2025

*Cost per mile is for the largest purchase tier and includes the 7.5% tax. We value AAdvantage miles at 1.5 cents each.

Promotion details last updated on November 27, 2026.

Unlike Delta SkyMiles and United MileagePlus, American AAdvantage continues to publish award charts for travel on partner airlines, and redemption rates are largely quite good, especially for travel in premium cabins on partner airlines. Among the “big three” carriers in the US, I tend to think AAdvantage has the best redemption opportunities.

I find the cost of business class redemptions to be excellent in many cases. There are instances where it could make sense to pick up miles during a promotion with a short term use in mind. Just to give a few examples of some of my favorite uses of AAdvantage miles (all redemption rates are one-way):

Now, unfortunately the catch is that partner award availability is in many instances quite limited. For airlines like Cathay Pacific, Etihad, and Qatar Airways, the airlines now largely restrict premium awards to members of their own frequent flyer programs. So definitely do your research before buying any miles.

Another thing worth mentioning is that if you redeem for travel on British Airways, get ready to pay huge carrier imposed surcharges, which could be hundreds of dollars on a long haul premium cabin trip. So that wouldn’t be my preferred use of American Airlines miles.

American Airlines belongs to the oneworld alliance, so you can redeem AAdvantage miles on all oneworld airlines.

On top of that, you can redeem miles on some of American’s other partner airlines, including Aer Lingus, Air Tahiti Nui, China Southern, Etihad Airways, and GOL Airlines, among others.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider AAdvantage miles to be worth 1.5 cents each. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from AAdvantage miles than that.

American AAdvantage miles don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 24 months. Eligible activity includes earning or redeeming AAdvantage miles in any quantity.

There are lots of great ways to earn American miles aside from outright buying them:

Through December 2, 2026, American AAdvantage is offering a discount on buying miles. The program is offering up to a 50% discount when you buy American Airlines miles, which is an opportunity to buy them for 1.88 cents each. While I wouldn’t speculatively buy miles at this cost, with a specific use in mind, there could be value with this offer.

Air travelers returning home from Thanksgiving can breathe a sigh of relief.

Flight schedules were close to normal on Friday after a series of storms snarled flights on both coasts during the run-up to Thanksgiving.

And Mother Nature appeared not to have any more major curveballs to throw at travelers between now and Sunday, normally one of the busiest air travel periods of the year as holiday-goers return home.

That came after more than 460 flights were canceled on Thursday, according to data from FlightAware. The bad weather complicated the plans of tens of thousands of travelers with flights on Thanksgiving Day. East Coast airports serving the metro areas of New York City, Washington, D.C., Boston, Philadelphia and Baltimore were the hardest hit, but disruptions rippled across airports in Florida, the Midwest and the West Coast.

The main culprit: A Thanksgiving Day coastal storm on the East Coast that was strong enough to cause the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in Midtown Manhattan.

This week's flight problems came after a chaotic few weeks for air travel in the U.S., which featured a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 — and then tech outages at two of the largest U.S. carriers.

Now, Mother Nature has interfered with holiday travelers' plans.

“The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen had told TPG entering the Thanksgiving rush.

We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

Major airlines rolled out weather-related rebooking policies for airports facing poor conditions:

While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself typically brings much smaller crowds to airports.

According to preliminary data from the Transportation Security Administration, Thursday was the single quietest day at U.S. airports in nearly five years.

The forecast looks favorable through Sunday as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

Entering the holiday rush, the TSA had projected more than 3 million passengers could fly on Nov. 29. That would be the first time U.S. passenger traffic would eclipse that mark in 2026.

Here are some things you should do if you've been affected by bad weather this holiday week, or plan to fly on the upcoming busy Sunday.

Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories (see above) that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

Take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

Just keep in mind: As more and more cities are affected by bad weather, disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

Have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:

Want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance plan for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.

#6095. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

#6094. Citi AAdvantage Executive Card Review: Is The Admirals Club Perk Worth It?

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (formerly known as the Citi AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard) is American Airlines’ most premium co-branded credit card, as part of the Citi partnership. While the Citi AA Executive Card has a steep annual fee, it offers strong perks, ranging from an Admirals Club membership, to the ability to supercharge your AAdvantage elite status, to credits that can help offset the annual fee.

If you ask me, it’s one of the best value premium airline credit cards out there, and it’s also the airline credit card with the strongest lounge access perks. While products like the American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) might typically be the first that come to mind when people consider premium cards, this one could make a lot more sense if you’re a frequent American flyer.

In this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at the Citi AA Executive Card, with my Citi AAdvantage Executive Card review. I think this is especially important in light of the card’s recent refresh, where we saw the annual fee increase, but also saw new perks added.

Link: Learn more about the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard®

Let me start by briefly summarizing the key details of the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card:

This is the ideal card if you value American Admirals Club lounge access, if you’re going for elite status with American AAdvantage, or if you can just make the credits on the card work. If you’re just an occasional American flyer, there are probably more affordable options that will be easier to justify in the long term. However, with the card’s big welcome bonus, there’s a huge incentive to give this card a try.

One of the reasons that you’ll want to consider applying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the excellent welcome bonus it has. Of course that has to be balanced with the annual fee, and you also have to take into account the eligibility requirements, so let’s go through those details for the Citi AA Executive Card.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card currently has a welcome bonus of 80,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $8,000 within the first three months.

Personally, I value American AAdvantage miles at ~1.5 cents each, so to me, those miles are worth about $1,200. That’s an excellent bonus, especially for a card that also offers a lot of value in the long run. There are so many great uses of AAdvantage miles, including for travel on partner airlines.

For what it’s worth, I value Delta SkyMiles at 1.1 cents each, and United MileagePlus miles at 1.3 cents each, so these are the most valuable miles among the “big three” carriers, based on my math.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card bonus miles aren’t available to those who have received a new cardmember bonus for this card in the past 48 months (however, you are eligible if you’ve had a different American Airlines credit card, including if you’ve received a bonus on a different product).

Then there are the typical rules for Citi credit card applications, including that you can apply for at most one card with Citi every eight days, and at most two cards every 65 days.

There’s not a consistent credit score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card has a $695 annual fee. There’s also a lot of value to adding authorized users (as I’ll discuss below). You can expect to pay a total of $175 for up to three authorized users (so potentially under $60 each), and then each authorized user after that costs $175.

Keep in mind that if you’re a Citigold customer, you can receive a $145 annual rebate on your annual fee, which is a nice perk.

When it comes to spending money on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, here’s the rewards structure:

In terms of the reward for spending, there are potentially better cards for purchasing airline tickets, and also better cards for everyday spending. However, keep in mind that the most compelling reason to spend money on the card is in order to earn elite status with American Airlines. American Airlines uses its Loyalty Points system for status qualification, and credit card spending can help you earn status.

American’s elite requirements are currently as follows, and you earn one Loyalty Point for every dollar spent on an American Airlines credit card:

Spending on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card could earn you elite status, which I know will interest many. That’s the primary reason you’ll want to consider this card for spending.

I do want to specifically point out one thing that throws people off — you earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on the card, unrelated to how many miles you earn for spending. In other words, if you’re making an American Airlines purchase, you’d earn 4x AAdvantage redeemable miles, but only 1x Loyalty Points on the purchase as such.

In addition to earning one Loyalty Point for every dollar spent on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can also earn up to 40,000 Loyalty Points every year just for being a cardmember:

In other words, if you have this card, you’d only otherwise need to earn 170,000 Loyalty Points for Executive Platinum status, since this card would get you a boost of 30,000 Loyalty Points at that level. Those Loyalty Points can be earned in a variety of ways, ranging from flying, to online shopping, to credit card spending, to booking vacation packages. Either way, this Loyalty Points boost would be quite the advantage in terms of qualifying for Loyalty Point Rewards, and even upgrade priority.

The AAdvantage elite qualifying year goes from the beginning of March until the end of February of the following year. You don’t need to have the card at the beginning of the year to take advantage of this, so even if you open the card during the membership year, you could still earn 40,000 bonus Loyalty Points for that year (in other words, the credits can be retroactive).

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this can be a good option for purchases abroad.

While you’ll want to consult the full cardmember agreement and guide to benefits, the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers useful travel protection, including trip cancellation coverage, trip interruption coverage, trip delay protection, lost baggage protection, rental car coverage, and more.

So this is a good card to potentially use for travel purchases, since you have to put them on your card to take advantage of those benefits.

One of the main reasons you may want to get the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the lounge access perks that the card offers. Having the Citi AA Executive Card is the best way to access Admirals Clubs. Let’s discuss how that works.

The primary cardmember on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card receives a full Admirals Club membership, including guesting privileges. That in and of itself is a reason this card makes sense.

While Admirals Clubs aren’t anything to get too excited about, they are improving nicely, in terms of design, and also in terms of the quality of food and beverages. I also appreciate the expansion of the Provisions by Admirals Club concept, whereby the airline offers Admirals Club members grab & go facility, where they can get some drinks or snacks to go before their flight.

Ordinarily, if you were to buy a comparable Admirals Club membership with guesting privileges, you’d pay a minimum of $1,200 per year.

By getting an Admirals Club membership with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you’re saving $505-705 right off the bat.

Note that while you can redeem miles for an Admirals Club membership, it’s a terrible value, as you’re getting only a cent per mile.

What you get with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is a full Admirals Club membership, so you don’t even have to bring your credit card, as your membership will be linked to your AAdvantage number:

Admirals Club members don’t get access to Flagship Lounges, as that access is determined based on the ticket you purchased rather than any membership.

Many people may be considering applying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card shortly before taking an American Airlines trip. How soon after being approved for the card does your Admirals Club membership kick in?

Since the primary cardmember gets a full Admirals Club membership, it’s linked to their AAdvantage account. Many may be surprised to learn that this membership could very well kick in before you even receive your credit card in the mail, and you don’t even need your card to enter a lounge.

Fortunately, there’s an easy way to tell if your Admirals Club membership has been activated. To figure it out, pretend that you’re signing up for an Admirals Club membership. Go to this page, enter your AAdvantage number, last name, and password.

If your account has already been updated to reflect the Admirals Club membership, you’ll see that the next page shows “1-Year Citi AADV Exec CC Membership.”

If it hasn’t been updated, you’ll see that it gives you the option of choosing what kind of membership you want to purchase.

Note that this only works for the primary cardmember. Since the authorized users don’t get a full Admirals Club membership, they wouldn’t show up as being eligible online. Authorized users need to present the physical Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, since there’s no membership linked to their AAdvantage account.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card also offers Admirals Club access for authorized users. As I explained above, you can add up to three authorized users for a total of $175, which potentially comes out to under $60 per authorized user. I’d say that’s a real sweet spot, since securing lounge access for friends and family for under $60 each is an amazing value.

Note that authorized users receive Admirals Club access and not a membership, so there are the restrictions:

For the purposes of accessing Admirals Clubs this is more or less the same as an outright membership.

Adding authorized users to the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is super easy, and can be done directly on Citi’s website. Follow this link to access the part of the Citi website where you add authorized users, and then log into your account.

On the next page, you’ll be able to manage authorized users, including adding and removing them.

You’ll just need their name to add them, and you have the choice of whether or not you want to give them permission to access your online account.

Make sure you trust all your authorized users, since any charges they incur will be your responsibility.

The primary reason to get the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the great welcome bonus, ability to earn status with spending, ability to receive 40,000 Loyalty Points annually just for being a cardmember, and Admirals Club benefit.

However, the Citi AA Executive Card offers some other perks that could add a lot of value for card members. These perks range from priority check-in at business class counters, to early boarding, to inflight or Admirals Club credits, to savings with American Airlines Vacations, Lyft, Avis, Budget, Global Entry, or TSA PreCheck, to elite status with Avis and Omni.

Below is what you need to know about all the other perks of the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card.

Those with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card receive a first checked bag free on domestic American Airlines itineraries not just for themselves, but also for up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation. There’s no need to actually pay for the ticket with your Citi AAdvantage Executive Card — you just have to make sure it’s linked to your AAdvantage account (this benefit applies for the primary cardmember only).

American ordinarily charges $45-50 for the first checked bag, so that’s a $90-100 value per person roundtrip (and if you had eight companions all checking a bag, that would be a value of $810-900).

One thing that sometimes throws off cardmembers is that this benefit doesn’t work for international flights, and it doesn’t work for a second bag, if your fare includes one bag. So just understand this is exclusively a first checked bag benefit on domestic flights.

For being the primary cardmember on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card you receive several valuable airport benefits, including priority check-in, priority airport screening, and early boarding. These are all features that can save you time and money.

There’s no need to show your card, as these perks should automatically be reflected with your ticket when you have your credit card linked to your AAdvantage account (which is automatic when you’re the primary cardmember).

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $500 in statement credits per calendar year toward American Airlines Vacations purchases. American Airlines Vacations is the carrier’s vacation package portal. This credit is semi-annual, meaning you can take advantage of a $250 credit every six months (once in January through June, and once in July through December).

This applies for a booking of two or more travel components, like a flight, car reservation, or hotel booking. Many people find American Airlines Vacations to be a great deal, and a good way to earn bonus Loyalty Points.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $200 in InKind credits every year. This comes in the form of a $100 semi-annual credit, with one being available January 1 through June 30, and the other being available July 1 through December 31. This can be used across multiple meals, and tips aren’t covered by the credit. Either the primary cardmember or authorized users can use the perk, though authorized users don’t get extra credits.

InKind is my favorite dining rewards app, and to me, this is basically good as cash. I dine at InKind restaurants constantly, as there are some really high quality restaurants on the list, so I value this new card perk immensely. If you’re new to InKind, make sure you also register through a refer-a-friend link, so you can get an extra credit.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $180 in Lyft credits every year. This comes in the form of a $15 Lyft credit each month after taking three eligible rides. The Lyft credit expires 30 days after it’s issued. Either the primary cardmember or authorized users can use the perk, though authorized users don’t get extra credits. Admittedly this requires quite a bit of effort to use, so not everyone will get value from that.

Just for having the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can receive up to $120 back on eligible Avis or Budget rentals every calendar year. Just charge an eligible pre-paid rental to your card each year, and you’ll receive a statement credit up to the $120 limit. This can be used toward a single rental or multiple rentals made directly with Avis or Budget. If you rent with Avis and Budget with any frequency, this could be worth face value.

Just for having the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can receive up to $100 in statement credits every calendar year toward spending onboard American flights, or in Admirals Clubs. So you can use this credit to purchase everything from premium drinks or snacks on flights, to premium alcoholic drinks in Admirals Clubs.

Just charge the eligible purchase to your card, and you’ll be reimbursed automatically, with no registration required.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit once every four years, which is worth up to $120. Simply charge the purchase to your card and it will automatically be reimbursed. You don’t have to be the one signing up — you can always pay for a friend or family member who is signing up instead.

Personally, I always recommend applying for Global Entry, because Global Entry automatically comes with TSA PreCheck, while the inverse isn’t true.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card now offers some perks with Omni Hotels & Resorts. For those not familiar, Omni operates around 50 properties in the United States and Canada, so there’s value in getting extra perks at these hotels. Specifically:

To take advantage of this, you’ll want to enroll before your stay, book your stay direct with Omni, and pay with the card. If you stay at Omni properties with any frequencies, this is quite a nice value-add, if you ask me.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers complimentary Avis President’s Club status, with enrollment available through August 31, 2028.

Avis President’s Club status offers a variety of perks, including car upgrades, expedited service, complimentary additional drivers, and more. If you rent from Avis, you should definitely be able to get some value from this.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is a World Legend Mastercard, meaning that it comes with quite a few benefits you may not be familiar with. In addition to the concierge service, there are also savings and other perks with a variety of businesses, ranging from DoorDash to HelloFresh.

Let me once again state that this card used to be known as the Citi AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard, before recently being rebranded as a World Legend Mastercard.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is a lucrative card that I personally have and also recommend, but only if you’re a frequent flyer with American. If you fly American with any frequency then an Admirals Club membership is valuable, and this is the best way to get an Admirals Club membership. There can even be value in adding up to three authorized users, which will cost a total of $175, as they’d get Admirals Club access as well.

In addition to lounge access, the Citi AA Executive Card offers up to 40,000 Loyalty Points per year (even without spending money on the card), which can make a big difference for anyone chasing status with American. Furthermore, the card potentially offers hundreds of dollars in credits per year, which can help offset the annual fee.

However, this isn’t a card that I’d use for my everyday spending unless I specifically valued the added Loyalty Points from spending. Otherwise, there are much more rewarding cards for everyday spending, and I’d just hold onto this card for the very strong perks, including lounge access, and the bonus Loyalty Points without a spending requirement.

For my mental accounting purposes, I take the $695 annual fee, and then subtract the $200 InKind credit, which I consider to basically be worth face value. That really takes the “out of pocket” on the card to $495 per year for me, which is an amazing deal for the Admirals Club membership and bonus Loyalty Points.

While the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is American’s most premium credit card, it’s also worth being aware of the Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® (learn more), which has a $350 annual fee. There are lots of reasons to consider that card, including an excellent welcome bonus. Among other things:

I think there’s potentially merit to having both cards, especially if you value earning the Loyalty Points bonuses. Otherwise I’d say the Citi AAdvantage Globe Card is easier to justify if you’re an occasional American flyer, while I think the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is easier to justify if you value an Admirals Club membership.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card isn’t for everyone. If you’re not a frequent flyer on American then you shouldn’t consider this card. However, if you are a frequent flyer on American then this card is totally for you.

While Admirals Clubs aren’t anything to get too excited about, there’s still huge value in the complimentary snacks and drinks, free Wi-Fi and quiet places to sit, and access to an agent in the event your flight has irregular operations.

Even beyond the Admirals Club membership, the card offers other useful perks, like the ability to earn Loyalty Points, priority services with American, and the ability to receive credits with American Airlines Vacations, InKind, Avis, Budget, Lyft, and more.

I’ve had the Citi AA Executive Card for years, and love it. If you don’t yet have the card, this is a good time to apply, given the offer that’s available.

This card is a no brainer for many and a no way for others. No brainer for me. If you live in a major metro area, the $200 inKind is as good as cash. It's not just sit down restaurants - my local coffee and pizza place are on inKind. Even if you value the $200 at $130 (can sometimes get discounted $100 inKind gift cards at costco for $64.99) it's still easy money. $120 Avis is easy to use, just can't stack with AA Cars. $100 F&B is an upgrade from 25% off F&B - will actually use that now. $250x2 off AA Vacations... look, it's not the most exciting credit out there, and I'd value it at $0 with any use of it being a bonus. I view it as max $200 off because with AA Vacations you basically have to pay $50/pp for the PDP cancellation protection, otherwise it's like buying basic economy. And it's really only useful for solo travel because otherwise you are sharing the miles/LP with the entire booking party. If you can use it, great, just have to run the math on whether it's actually saving you money. I think if AA does not extend the MaximizeMiles promotion on it (currently expires 12/31, they extended it from 9/30...), it makes the math much harder. For me the sweet spot is AA Hotels / AA Cars. AA Hotels though - you can really get an incredible amount of miles/LP if you have any AA card and any AA status. Plus 12x on spend on the card - it's really fantastic. #6093. Is Lufthansa Really Hiring 1,000 Pilots By 2033 While Cutting 1,000 Hub Jobs?

Lufthansa has made headlines in recent weeks for multiple potential moves that would impact its workforce. On the one hand, proposed cuts could eat into its workforce at its two key hubs, Frankfurt Main Airport (FRA) and Munich Airport (MUC). On the other, an offer has been tabled that would guarantee new pilot hires ahead if accepted.

Each respective proposal involves reducing or adding the same number of staff members as the other. It would appear, therefore, that Lufthansa — Europe’s largest airline by fleet count — is heading toward two fairly drastic efforts that would see one area slimmed down for the other to be bolstered by equal measure. The reality is far more complex, though. While there is a sense of irony behind the overall thinking, each decision stems from an entirely isolated issue the carrier is navigating today. So, what is really happening?

On paper, yes, Lufthansa has suggested both cutting 1,000 jobs and hiring 1,000 pilots. Proposals put forward by Lufthansa to employees internally include the cuts, as reported initially around November 19. In contrast, proposals made to pilot union Vereinigung Cockpit and detailed by Lufthansa just a few days earlier on November 17 would see the airline commit to recruiting the pilots over the coming years.

The thinking behind each decision is not so straightforward, however. Cuts appear to have been tabled on the back of Lufthansa’s own deteriorating financial performance. In contrast, Lufthansa offering to hire new pilots looks to be an attempt to break a stalemate with the union that has followed months of talks. As such, the two are not necessarily completely interlinked.

Nonetheless, were both to materialize, it would indeed leave the airline in a position where it is reducing its workforce in one area, while bolstering it in another. It is unclear whether either will in fact materialize, with Lufthansa telling Simple Flying it had “nothing to add to these media reports” when approached for comment. What is clear is that this year has been tough on carriers, and heated union negotiations have added another headache in Lufthansa’s case.

The reasoning given behind the cuts is a worsening financial performance currently, not least due to rising fuel prices. In the letter to employees, obtained by the German Press Agency and reported on by various outlets, the airline’s board clearly laid out its intentions.

“At the Frankfurt and Munich hubs, we are planning to cut a total of 1,000 full-time positions within the Lufthansa Airlines subgroup,” the letter — signed by chief executive Jens Ritter among others — said. “Lufthansa Airlines is currently not competitive [and] we have reached a point where we need to make even more far-reaching changes,” it added.

Lufthansa Group financial highlights covering nine months to September 30:

The group’s latest financial results, released on November 3, backed up the bleak diagnosis. Stronger revenue and income during the first nine months of the year were clouded by higher operating expenses. Notably, fuel costs rocketed 21% to €6.7 billion ($7.4 billion), despite hedging and reduced consumption, including as flight and passenger numbers fell by 4% and 1%, respectively. As for subsidiary Lufthansa Airlines — where cuts are planned — an adjusted pre-tax loss of €180 million ($198 million) was recorded, against a profit of €147 million ($162 million) a year prior.

The cuts, which apply until October, will impact short-haul flights.

So, simply put, Lufthansa has found itself grappling with a deteriorating underlying performance at a group level, with its flagship business slipping into the red. It is in this context that staff reductions within the latter were floated to employees. But unfortunately for the carrier, that makes up just one of the areas where pressure has been building.

The years-long dispute with Vereinigung Cockpit — which initially related to pension scheme changes dating back to 2017, but has since evolved to cover the likes of job progression and security — has only added to its woes. Owing to the deadlock between the two, the union called pilot strikes at the carrier in February, March, and April. Subsequent second-quarter results from Lufthansa detailed that the industrial action had cost it at least €150 million ($165 million), and that six days' worth of strikes in April knocked capacity down 3%. Despite work towards a resolution since, talks between Vereinigung Cockpit and Lufthansa have collapsed recently.

Key dates from a packed November of Lufthansa-related news:

Third-quarter figures show worsening underlying performance at Lufthansa.

Period of mediation between Lufthansa and Vereinigung Cockpit ends.

Vereinigung Cockpit “prepared to begin working on the details of proposal”.

Lufthansa publishes counteroffer instead, including promise of up to 1,000 cockpit hires.

Vereinigung Cockpit also signals obligation to refrain from strikes has expired.

Reports emerge Lufthansa planning 1,000 job cuts at key hubs.

Vereinigung Cockpit-imposed deadline for Lufthansa to return to talks passes.

Vereinigung Cockpit slams Lufthansa in a statement. No strikes announced.

A period of arbitration was followed by one of mediation that ended in mid-November, at which point a deal emerged that the union backed but the airline did not. Lufthansa instead tabled a counteroffer, which it said was based on arbitrators’ recommendations and included the proposal of 1,000 new cockpit hires. Vereinigung Cockpit responded in turn by setting a deadline of November 23 for the airline to withdraw it and return to the negotiating table, which then passed to no avail. That left the union to slam the airline the day after, when it wrote: “Seven months of exploratory talks, three rounds of conciliation, and a total of 18 rounds of discussions with the mediator have apparently been in vain.”

Whether the prospect of job cuts was raised because negotiations were reaching a tipping point has been questioned by Vereinigung Cockpit. “Coincidence? Hardly,” it noted in response to reports of the cuts, “what is being built up here is primarily a lot of threatening talk”. That said, it is no secret that the wider aviation industry has faced struggles this year.

KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, another European carrier, said in early November it would look to reduce its workforce by 15% in response to an “increasingly complex” operational environment. Shortly after, Australia’s Qantas signaled it would be cutting 850 corporate roles and outsourcing the work overseas.

Such measures are being taken in each case against the backdrop of a sustained increase in fuel prices since the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East earlier this year. To put that into perspective, the price of jet fuel averaged 71.9% more over the week to November 20 than it did in the same period a year before, per the International Air Transport Association. Needless to say, ballooning costs have been an issue for airlines globally of late.

Most of the cuts will impact German workers in administrative roles.

Unsurprisingly, Lufthansa did refer to such cost pressures upon telling staff of the cuts, writing: “The price of fuel exposes and exacerbates [...] structural weaknesses.” As with its offer to Vereinigung Cockpit, though, there are several questions over what actually comes next.

November’s third-quarter figures detailed that Lufthansa Airlines had 39,622 employees as of the end of September, meaning a reduction of 1,000 positions would mark a 2.5% cut to its workforce. Though stark, the results also showed there had been a 0.9% drop — equivalent to 341 employees — in headcount at the subsidiary since a year earlier. Aside from impacting “full-time positions,” Lufthansa has yet to detail how the roles will be axed, which will be affected, and over what timeline. Companies can avoid directly slashing jobs more gradually through attrition, for instance, a tool KLM said it was to use. Another thing to flag is Lufthansa’s announcement last year that 4,000 administrative positions were to go, and so whether the latest round of cuts would be linked to these remains to be seen.

As for its offer to create new cockpit positions, the headline figure of 1,000 new pilot hires arguably implies a more drastic expansion on Lufthansa's part than would actually materialize. The promised recruitment drive runs through 2033, giving the airline several years to fill the positions. However, previous figures from pilots' union Vereinigung Cockpit, cited by Aviation Direct, point to hundreds of age-related departures over the same period. Around 300 retirements are anticipated in 2026 and 2027 alone, with a further 740 expected between 2029 and 2034. Note that these cover both Lufthansa Classic — where the additions would be made — and Lufthansa Cargo. Either way, they suggest much of the recruitment could simply be needed anyway to replace departing personnel.

That could be by design, of course, with Lufthansa’s cost-saving efforts potentially set to go as far as reducing its mainline narrowbody fleet in favor of buoying long-haul operations. Ultimately, though, time will tell what comes next.

Indeed, Lufthansa has told staff 1,000 positions are to go. It has also floated the idea of committing to hiring 1,000 pilots in the coming years. Details of the former remain few and far between, however. The latter, meanwhile, has by no means been met with enthusiasm from the union it was designed to win over.

#6092. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

#6091. Ryanair Now Withholds Free Seats Until Just Before Departure, Blames Customer Feedback

Ryanair has quietly updated its policy for how it assigns seats to those people who don’t pay the seat assignment fee, as reported by The Irish Times. While I wouldn’t consider this to be anything unreasonable, what I’m amused by is the carrier’s justification. The airline claims that it’s doing this due to customer feedback, rather than to generate more revenue.

Ryanair is known for being an unapologetic ultra low cost carrier. The airline has low base fares, and then charges fees for just about everything. Among other things, the airline charges to assign seats in advance, and those who don’t pay for specific seat assignments are just randomly assigned seats (and often in a rather punitive way).

However, the way the airline is randomly allocating seats has quietly changed as of late October 2026, coinciding with the start of the winter schedule. Historically, the airline has automatically assigned seats to passengers without seat assignments around 24 hours before departure.

Some passengers seemed to “game” this, and would essentially “gamble.” What they’d do is wait until 24 hours out to see what seat they were assigned for free. Then if they weren’t happy with their automatic seat assignment, they could still pay to assign a better seat.

Under the new policy, the airline still issues a boarding pass up to 24 hours out, but without a seat assignment. Then the boarding pass automatically shows the seat assignment within four hours of departure.

The logic here seems pretty clear — some people do care somewhat about where they sit, but want to avoid fees if they can. By withholding seat assignments until hours before departure, passengers are presumably more likely to pay for seat assignments in advance, to avoid that uncertainty.

Ryanair has confirmed this seat assignment policy change in a statement, sharing that “the timing of the allocation of free random seats is determined at all times by the airline.” Right, nobody disputes that the airline has the right to do this.

So, what’s the logic for this policy change? According to the airline, it’s “to allow those passengers who wish to select their preferred seat more time to do so. We had a number of complaints this summer that passengers could not book their preferred seat on the day of travel as it had been already randomly allocated as a free seat up to 24 hours prior to departure.”

The Ryanair representative went on to say that “passengers who choose a free of charge random seat clearly don’t mind where they sit, and their digital boarding pass is automatically updated between three to four hours prior to departure, which is well before they arrive at either their departure airport or their boarding gate.”

Ryanair is of course within its rights to have this policy, but I think the logic is pretty obvious, and it’s to generate more revenue. After all, 24 hours out people would see what they were randomly assigned at online check-in, and would still have a lot of choices if they wanted to pay for seats, since most people don’t check-in online exactly at the 24-hour mark.

But within a few hours of departure, virtually everyone has checked in online, and not many seats will be left. So I imagine the goal is to condition more customers to pay for seat assignments in advance. I love the claim that customers complained that their preferred seats on the day of travel were randomly allocated to others for free:

Ryanair has a new policy for automatic seat allocations. In the past, the airline would automatically assign seats to passengers 24 hours out, giving them quite the window to “gamble” on the free seat assignment, and then pay for a different seat assignment if they weren’t happy with the free one.

The airline has now started only assigning free seats at most four hours out. The airline claims that this is due to customer feedback, so that passengers have more time to assign their choice of paid seats. However, I imagine that’s not quite accurate, and this is instead about conditioning people to pay for seat assignments, rather than “gambling” on the free allocations.

What do you make of this Ryanair seating policy change?

Welcome to “What’s in My Bag,” a new series where TPG staffers open their carry-ons, personal items and dopp kits to share the travel essentials they never leave home without. First up: The Points Guy founder, Brian Kelly.

As a travel expert who’s constantly on the go, I will say some of my favorite things that you’ll find in my bag revolve around staying organized and being comfortable — I always know where my essentials are. At this stage of my life, I’m willing to splurge a bit on handcrafted or well-made products that last. Quality is nonnegotiable.

This travel pouch is so chic, but definitely a splurge. It’s made with Saffiano leather and Re-Nylon, an innovative fabric that’s produced from recycled plastic recovered from the ocean. You can find it at Saks Fifth Avenue. I love it for keeping everything I might need on the go organized — with two top zipper pockets and one each on the front and back, I never run out of room.

Buy: Prada Re-Nylon and Saffiano leather travel pouch, $1,120

These Bose noise-canceling headphones are comfortable and seamlessly connect via Bluetooth. Plus, they are stylish and have great sound quality. The surround sound is awesome.

Buy: Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones, from $349 (normally $449)

As a content creator, I needed a good lav microphone with an iPhone receiver for when I’m out and about. The Rode wireless mic is super easy to use, holds a charge all day and slips right into my travel pouch.

Buy: Rode ultra-compact wireless microphone system with USB-C connector, $89 (normally $99)

My go-to quick snack is Quest protein peanut butter cups — indulgent yet packed with protein. I keep Grüns gummies in my bag for a healthy mix of essential vitamins and prebiotics. They keep me feeling energized and are more than just a multivitamin — they’re made with whole fruits and veggies too.

Buy: Grüns sugar-free gummies (pack of 28), $73.32; Quest protein peanut butter cups (pack of 12), $28.49

I firmly believe in investing in pieces that will last, and this handcrafted leather wallet from Aspinal of London is no exception. It holds up to eight cards and can be personalized with your initials.

Buy: Aspinal of London 8-card billfold wallet in black woven leather, $180 (normally $355)

I have a second phone for travel that’s connected to the T-Mobile network as a backup, and, depending on your service plan, T-Mobile also offers free Wi-Fi on U.S. airlines. I keep my main phone on Verizon, but you never want to be stuck without a phone when abroad.

I’m a big tennis fan, whether it’s traveling for a match or catching the U.S. Open when it's in New York. This easy-to-adjust hat is perfect to keep in my bag, so I always have one on me for sun protection.

Buy: Wimbledon Mono-tone Herringbone Cap, $64

Fashionable sun protection is a no-brainer. I love these Tom Ford sunglasses in black.

Buy: Tom Ford Snowdon sunglasses, $284 (normally $316)

This small device is super versatile — not only does it convert 220–240V AC input to 120V AC output, but it also includes five plug adapters so I can use it in nearly every country in the world.

Buy: Insignia international converter and plug adapters, $17.49 (normally $29.99)

This portable power bank gives me peace of mind knowing I can charge my phone on the go. Small and lightweight, it fits on the back of my iPhone without covering the camera and fits easily into my pocket or travel pouch.

Buy: UGreen 10000mAh 22.5W compact power bank, $19.99 (normally $29.99)

Obviously this promotion isn’t for everyone, but if you have any travel to potentially plan over the promotion period, then this offer is seriously worth considering. It’s awesome how often Southwest offers this promotion.

#6087. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
